studyMetadata.title: Exploring Deuteronomy
studyMetadata.subtitle: Bible Study
studyMetadata.description: A walk through Moses’ final sermon to Israel on the edge of the Promised Land. Each chapter has Bible questions tied to the passage, a short check on your answer, and personal reflections.
studyMetadata.author: Julie Rowbory

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 1-3: Disobedience Only Leads to Failure

elements.text: Deuteronomy is not primarily a law book. It is a sermon — or rather, three sermons, a song, and a blessing, all delivered by Moses on the plains of Moab, with the Promised Land visible in the distance. The people are about to cross the Jordan. Moses is not going with them. And so he speaks.

His opening sermon begins with history — but not all of it. Moses selects two episodes of rebellion, and the faithfulness of God that surrounded them on every side. He is not writing a chronicle; he is making a case. The generation standing before him is about to face the same test their parents failed. Moses wants them to choose differently.
As you read, watch for what Moses chooses to include — and what the pattern of those choices reveals about what he wants his hearers to understand.

elements.question: Read this section of the passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
1This is what Moses said to all of Israel in the Transjordanian wilderness, the arid rift valley opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Di Zahab. 2Now it is ordinarily an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Kadesh Barnea by way of Mount Seir. 3However, it was not until the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year that Moses addressed the Israelites just as the Lord had instructed him to do. 4This took place after the defeat of King Sihon of the Amorites, whose capital was in Heshbon, and King Og of Bashan, whose capital was in Ashtaroth, specifically in Edrei. 5So it was in the Transjordan, in Moab, that Moses began to deliver these words:

6The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb and said, “You have stayed in the area of this mountain long enough. 7Head out and resume your journey. Enter the Amorite hill country, and all its neighboring areas, including the rift valley, the hill country, the foothills, the Negev, and the coastal plain—all of Canaan and Lebanon as far as the Great River, that is, the Euphrates. 8Look! I have already given the land to you. Go, occupy the territory that I, the Lord, promised to give to your ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants.” 9I also said to you at that time, “I am no longer able to sustain you by myself. 10The Lord your God has increased your population to the point that you are now as numerous as the very stars of the sky. 11Indeed, may the Lord, the God of your ancestors, make you a thousand times more numerous than you are now, blessing you just as he said he would! 12But how can I alone bear up under the burden of your hardship and strife? 13Select wise and practical men, those known among your tribes, whom I may appoint as your leaders.” 14You replied to me that what I had said to you was good. 15So I chose as your tribal leaders wise and well-known men, placing them over you as administrators of groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and also as other tribal officials. 16I furthermore admonished your judges at that time that they should pay attention to issues among your fellow citizens and judge fairly, whether between one person and a native Israelite or a resident foreigner. 17They must not discriminate in judgment, but hear the lowly and the great alike. Nor should they be intimidated by human beings, for judgment belongs to God. If the matter being adjudicated is too difficult for them, they should bring it before me for a hearing.

18So I instructed you at that time regarding everything you should do. 19Then we left Horeb and passed through all that immense, forbidding wilderness that you saw on the way to the Amorite hill country as the Lord our God had commanded us to do, finally arriving at Kadesh Barnea. 20Then I said to you, “You have come to the Amorite hill country, which the Lord our God is about to give us. 21Look, he has placed the land in front of you! Go up, take possession of it, just as the Lord, the God of your ancestors, said to do. Do not be afraid or discouraged!” 22So all of you approached me and said, “Let’s send some men ahead of us to scout out the land and bring us back word as to how we should attack it and what the cities are like there.” 23I thought this was a good idea, so I sent twelve men from among you, one from each tribe. 24They left and went up to the hill country, coming to the Eshcol Valley, which they scouted out. 25Then they took some of the produce of the land and carried it back down to us. They also brought a report to us, saying, “The land that the Lord our God is about to give us is good.”

26You were not willing to go up, however, but instead rebelled against the Lord your God. 27You complained among yourselves privately and said, “Because the Lord hates us he brought us from Egypt to deliver us over to the Amorites so they could destroy us! 28What is going to happen to us? Our brothers have drained away our courage by describing people who are more numerous and taller than we are, and great cities whose defenses appear to be as high as heaven itself! Moreover, they said they saw Anakites there.” 29So I responded to you, “Do not be terrified of them! 30The Lord your God is about to go ahead of you; he will fight for you, just as you saw him do in Egypt 31and in the wilderness, where you saw him carrying you along like a man carries his son. This he did everywhere you went until you came to this very place.” 32However, through all this you did not have confidence in the Lord your God, 33who would go before you on the way to find places for you to camp, appearing in a fire at night and in a cloud by day to show you the way you ought to go.

34When the Lord heard you, he became angry and made this vow: 35“Not a single person of this evil generation will see the good land that I promised to give to your ancestors! 36The exception is Caleb son of Jephunneh; he will see it and I will give him and his descendants the territory on which he has walked, because he has wholeheartedly followed me.” 37As for me, the Lord was also angry with me on your account. He said, “You also will not be able to go there. 38However, Joshua son of Nun, your assistant, will go. Encourage him, because he will enable Israel to inherit the land. 39Also, your infants, who you thought would die on the way, and your children, who as yet do not know good from bad, will go there; I will give them the land and they will possess it. 40But as for you, turn back and head for the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea.”

41Then you responded to me and admitted, “We have sinned against the Lord. We will now go up and fight as the Lord our God has told us to do.” So you each put on your battle gear and prepared to go up to the hill country. 42But the Lord told me: “Tell them this: ‘Do not go up and fight, because I will not be with you and you will be defeated by your enemies.’” 43I spoke to you, but you did not listen. Instead you rebelled against the Lord and recklessly went up to the hill country. 44The Amorite inhabitants of that area confronted you and chased you like a swarm of bees, striking you down from Seir as far as Hormah. 45Then you came back and wept before the Lord, but he paid no attention to you whatsoever. 46Therefore, you remained at Kadesh for a long time—indeed, for the full time.

elements.question: Read the second section of the passage…
elements.answer:
1Then we turned and set out toward the wilderness on the way to the Red Sea just as the Lord told me to do, detouring around Mount Seir for a long time. 2At this point the Lord said to me, 3“You have circled around this mountain long enough; now turn north. 4Instruct these people as follows: ‘You are about to cross the border of your relatives the descendants of Esau, who inhabit Seir. They will be afraid of you, so watch yourselves carefully. 5Do not be hostile toward them, because I am not giving you any of their land, not even a footprint, for I have given Mount Seir as an inheritance for Esau. 6You may purchase food to eat and water to drink from them. 7All along the way I, the Lord your God, have blessed your every effort. I have been attentive to your travels through this great wilderness. These forty years I have been with you; you have lacked nothing.’”

8So we turned away from our relatives the descendants of Esau, the inhabitants of Seir, turning from the route of the rift valley which comes up from Elat and Ezion Geber, and traveling the way of the wilderness of Moab. 9Then the Lord said to me, “Do not harass Moab and provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land as your territory. This is because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession. 10(The Emites used to live there, a people as powerful, numerous, and tall as the Anakites. 11These people, as well as the Anakites, are also considered Rephaites; the Moabites call them Emites. 12Previously the Horites lived in Seir, but the descendants of Esau dispossessed and destroyed them and settled in their place, just as Israel did to the land it came to possess, the land the Lord gave them.) 13Now, get up and cross the Wadi Zered.” So we did so. 14Now the length of time it took for us to go from Kadesh Barnea to the crossing of Wadi Zered was thirty-eight years, time for all the military men of that generation to die, just as the Lord had vowed to them. 15Indeed, it was the very hand of the Lord that eliminated them from within the camp until they were all gone.

16So it was that after all the military men had been eliminated from the community, 17the Lord said to me, 18“Today you are going to cross the border of Moab, that is, of Ar. 19But when you come close to the Ammonites, do not harass or provoke them because I am not giving you any of the Ammonites’ land as your possession; I have already given it to Lot’s descendants as their possession.”

20(That also is considered to be a land of the Rephaites. The Rephaites lived there originally; the Ammonites call them Zamzummites. 21They are a people as powerful, numerous, and tall as the Anakites. But the Lord destroyed the Rephaites in advance of the Ammonites, so they dispossessed them and settled down in their place. 22This is exactly what he did for the descendants of Esau who lived in Seir when he destroyed the Horites before them so that they could dispossess them and settle in their area to this very day. 23As for the Avvites who lived in settlements as far west as Gaza, Caphtorites who came from Crete destroyed them and settled down in their place.)

elements.question: Read the final section of the passage…
elements.answer:
12This is the land we brought under our control at that time: The territory extending from Aroer by the Wadi Arnon and half the Gilead hill country with its cities I gave to the Reubenites and Gadites. 13The rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to half the tribe of Manasseh. (All the region of Argob, that is, all Bashan, is called the land of Rephaim. 14Jair, son of Manasseh, took all the Argob region as far as the border with the Geshurites and Maacathites —namely Bashan—and called it by his name, Havvoth Jair, which it retains to this very day.) 15I gave Gilead to Machir. 16To the Reubenites and Gadites I allocated the territory extending from Gilead as far as Wadi Arnon (the exact middle of the wadi was a boundary) all the way to the Wadi Jabbok, the Ammonite border. 17The rift valley and the Jordan River were also a border, from the Sea of Kinnereth to the sea of the rift valley (that is, the Salt Sea), beneath the slopes of Pisgah to the east.

18At that time I instructed you as follows: “The Lord your God has given you this land for your possession. You warriors are to cross over equipped for battle before your fellow Israelites. 19But your wives, children, and livestock (of which I know you have many) may remain in the cities I have given you. 20You must fight until the Lord gives your countrymen victory as he did you and they take possession of the land that the Lord your God is giving them on the other side of the Jordan River. Then each of you may return to his own territory that I have given you.” 21I also commanded Joshua at the same time, “You have seen everything the Lord your God did to these two kings; he will do the same to all the kingdoms where you are going. 22Do not be afraid of them, for the Lord your God will personally fight for you.”

23Moreover, at that time I pleaded with the Lord, 24“O, Sovereign Lord, you have begun to show me your greatness and strength. (What god in heaven or earth can rival your works and mighty deeds?) 25Let me please cross over to see the good land on the other side of the Jordan River—this good hill country and the Lebanon!” 26But the Lord was angry at me because of you and would not listen to me. Instead, he said to me, “Enough of that! Do not speak to me anymore about this matter. 27Go up to the top of Pisgah and take a good look to the west, north, south, and east, for you will not be allowed to cross the Jordan. 28Commission Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, because he will lead these people over and will enable them to inherit the land you will see.” 29So we settled down in the valley opposite Beth Peor.

elements.question: Moses is about to retell Israel’s history before they enter the Promised Land. Before looking at the details, what impression does the overall shape of chapters 1-3 make on you? What kind of history is Moses recounting?

elements.text: 1:1-5: The Setting

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>This is what Moses said to the assembly of Israel in the Transjordanian wastelands, the arid country opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Di Zahab <sup>2</sup>Now it is ordinarily an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Kadesh Barnea by way of Mount Seir. <sup>3</sup>However, it was not until the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year that Moses addressed the Israelites just as the Lord had instructed him to do. <sup>4</sup>This took place after the defeat of King Sihon of the Amorites, whose capital was in Heshbon, and King Og of Bashan, whose capital was in Ashtaroth, specifically in Edrei. <sup>5</sup>So it was in the Transjordan, in Moab, that Moses began to deliver these words:

elements.question: Where and when is Moses speaking, and why do those details matter?
elements.sampleAnswer: The people are camped east of the Jordan, in the wilderness, on the very edge of the Promised Land. It is the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, so the crossing is close and Moses is near the end of his life. The note in v2 that the journey from Horeb to Kadesh Barnea takes eleven days hints at how much longer the people took than they should have. In this setting Moses begins to explain the law to a new generation, and his words are urgent and pastoral rather than abstract.
elements.questionHint: Look at the place and time in vv1–3, and at what Moses begins to do in v5.
elements.mainPoint: Moses speaks **at the edge of the land, forty years on**, to explain God’s law to the generation about to cross.

elements.text: 1:6-18: Leadership of the People of God

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb and said, “You have stayed in the area of this mountain long enough. <sup>7</sup>Get up now, resume your journey, heading for the Amorite hill country, to all its areas including the arid country, the highlands, the Shephelah, the Negev, and the coastal plain – all of Canaan and Lebanon as far as the Great River, that is, the Euphrates. <sup>8</sup>Look! I have already given the land to you. Go, occupy the territory that I, the Lord, promised to give to your ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants.” <sup>9</sup>I also said to you at that time, “I am no longer able to sustain you by myself. <sup>10</sup>The Lord your God has increased your population to the point that you are now as numerous as the very stars of the sky. <sup>11</sup>Indeed, may the Lord, the God of your ancestors, make you a thousand times more numerous than you are now, blessing you just as he said he would! <sup>12</sup>But how can I alone bear up under the burden of your hardship and strife? <sup>13</sup>Select wise and practical men, those known among your tribes, whom I may appoint as your leaders.” <sup>14</sup>You replied to me that what I had said to you was good. <sup>15</sup>So I chose as your tribal leaders wise and well-known men, placing them over you as administrators of groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and also as other tribal officials. <sup>16</sup>I furthermore admonished your judges at that time that they should pay attention to issues among your fellow citizens and judge fairly, whether between one citizen and another or a citizen and a resident foreigner. <sup>17</sup>They must not discriminate in judgment, but hear the lowly and the great alike. Nor should they be intimidated by human beings, for judgment belongs to God. If the matter being adjudicated is too difficult for them, they should bring it before me for a hearing. <sup>18</sup>So I instructed you at that time regarding everything you should do.

elements.question: What do vv6–8 show us about the character of God?
elements.sampleAnswer: God is the initiator: he tells the people they have stayed at the mountain long enough and directs them where to go. He is not distant or passive but actively ordering the life of his people and defining the extent of the land. He grounds it all in his promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. In v8 he speaks of the land as already given, so his command to go rests on his prior commitment. This is a God who speaks, directs, promises and keeps his word.
elements.questionHint: Look at what God says he has already done in v8, and at who is giving the commands in vv6–7.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Verses 9-18 may seem like an organisational aside about appointing judges. But what does it reveal about what God values for his people? How do justice and fair leadership reflect something about God’s own character?

elements.mainPoint: God commands from a position of promise: he has **already given the land**, so his people can go in his strength.

elements.text: 1:19-46: Disobedience and Failure

elements.question: In vv19–21, what does Moses tell the people to do, and what reasons does he give?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses tells the people to go up and take possession of the land. The reasons are that the Lord is giving it to them, that he promised it to their ancestors, and that they should not be afraid or discouraged. The argument is entirely God-centred: they should go because God has given. Obedience here is not blind compliance but a trusting response to a God who has already shown he can be relied on.
elements.questionHint: Look at what the Lord has done and promised in vv20–21, and at what Moses says not to do.
elements.mainPoint: Israel is told to go up because **the Lord has given the land**; obedience rests on his gift and promise, not on their strength.

elements.question: What lay at the root of the people’s first rebellion (vv26–28), and how does Moses answer it (vv29–33)?
elements.sampleAnswer: The first rebellion was the refusal to go up at Kadesh Barnea. The people were paralysed by the report of strong inhabitants, but their complaint in v27 shows the deeper problem: they said the Lord hated them and had brought them out of Egypt to destroy them. That is a catastrophic misreading of God’s character. Moses answers by reminding them of everything God has already done: he fought for them in Egypt, carried them like a father carries his son, and went before them in fire and cloud. The argument is that God’s track record gives no reason to doubt him now.
elements.questionHint: Read the people’s own words in v27, then see what Moses reminds them of in vv30–33.
elements.mainPoint: The rebellion at Kadesh was **a failure to trust God’s character**, and Moses answers it by pointing to what God has already done.

elements.question: What was the punishment for the first rebellion, and what shows God’s love even in judgment?
elements.sampleAnswer: The punishment is severe: the rebellious generation will not see the land God promised. Only Caleb, who followed the Lord fully, and Joshua are exempted. Even Moses is caught up in the consequences. Yet God’s love shows in what he does not do: he does not abandon his promise. The children the people feared would become plunder are the ones who will inherit the land, so the promise is delayed a generation rather than cancelled.
elements.questionHint: Notice who is exempted in vv36–38 and what is said about the children in v39.
elements.mainPoint: Judgment is real, but **God keeps his promise alive** through Caleb, Joshua and the children.

elements.question: How does the second rebellion (vv41–46) differ from the first, and what lay at its root?
elements.sampleAnswer: The second rebellion mirrors the first. Having refused to go up when God commanded it, the people now decide to go up when he has told them not to. They arm themselves and march out despite Moses’ warning that the Lord is not with them. The root of the first was fear; the root of the second is presumption, as if disobedience can be undone by acting as though it never happened. Both are failures of trust, and both end in defeat.
elements.questionHint: Compare what the people refused to do the first time with what they insist on doing in vv41–43.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Moses summarises the causes of the Israelites’ rebellion across chapter 1 as fear, doubting God’s goodness, and presumption. Can you see how these three things are related to each other at the root? What is the single underlying failure they all share?

elements.mainPoint: Fearful refusal and presumptuous action look like opposites but are **two forms of the same failure to trust God**.

elements.question: How does Moses sum up the forty years in the wilderness (v7), and why does he include this summary?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses says the Lord has blessed their every effort, watched over their travels through the great wilderness, and been with them for forty years, so that they lacked nothing. This is said of the very years of judgment, while the old generation was dying out. The summary is pastoral and forward-looking: if God provided for a rebellious generation, the new generation can trust him for what lies ahead.
elements.questionHint: Notice what the Lord says he has done ‘all along the way’ and what the people have lacked.
elements.mainPoint: Even in the years of judgment **the Lord was with his people and provided for them**, which is a reason to trust him now.

elements.question: What was Israel meant to learn from the way God dealt with Edom, Moab and Ammon?
elements.sampleAnswer: God had already given land to Esau’s descendants in Edom and to Lot’s descendants in Moab and Ammon, driving out the peoples who lived there before. These nations were not in covenant with him, so the Lord is not a local god limited to Israel’s affairs but the sovereign Lord of all nations. Israel is told not to provoke them because that land is not theirs to take. If God has done this for others, Israel can be sure he will give them the land he promised them.
elements.questionHint: Notice who gave each nation its land and what happened to the peoples who lived there before.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Moses is building a picture of a God who is sovereign not just over Israel but over all of history and all the nations. How does that vision of God’s sovereignty relate to the specific fears the people had expressed in chapter 1 — that the Anakites were too tall, the cities too fortified? Does the scale of God’s sovereignty shrink those obstacles, or does it feel abstract?

elements.mainPoint: The Lord who is about to give Israel Canaan has **already given other nations their lands**, so his rule is not limited to Israel.

elements.text: 3:12-29: Entering the Land

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>This is the land we brought under our control at that time: The territory extending from Aroer by the Wadi Arnon and half the Gilead hill country with its cities I gave to the Reubenites and Gadites. <sup>13</sup>The rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to half the tribe of Manasseh. (All the region of Argob, that is, all Bashan, is called the land of Rephaim. <sup>14</sup>Jair, son of Manasseh, took all the Argob region as far as the border with the Geshurites and Maacathites (namely Bashan) and called it by his name, Havvoth-Jair, which it retains to this very day.) <sup>15</sup>I gave Gilead to Machir. <sup>16</sup>To the Reubenites and Gadites I allocated the territory extending from Gilead as far as Wadi Arnon (the exact middle of the wadi was a boundary) all the way to the Wadi Jabbok, the Ammonite border. <sup>17</sup>The Arabah and the Jordan River were also a border, from the sea of Chinnereth to the sea of the Arabah (that is, the Salt Sea), beneath the watershed of Pisgah to the east. <sup>18</sup>At that time I instructed you as follows: ‘The Lord your God has given you this land for your possession. You warriors are to cross over before your fellow Israelites equipped for battle. <sup>19</sup>But your wives, children, and livestock (of which I know you have many) may remain in the cities I have given you. <sup>20</sup>You must fight until the Lord gives your countrymen victory as he did you and they take possession of the land that the Lord your God is giving them on the other side of the Jordan River. Then each of you may return to his own territory that I have given you.’ <sup>21</sup>I also commanded Joshua at the same time, ‘You have seen everything the Lord your God did to these two kings; he will do the same to all the kingdoms where you are going. <sup>22</sup>Do not be afraid of them, for the Lord your God will personally fight for you.’

elements.question: The Reubenites and Gadites already have their land. What are they still told to do (vv18–20), and what does this say about the people of God?
elements.sampleAnswer: Although they have received their inheritance, the Reubenites and Gadites must cross the Jordan armed ahead of their fellow Israelites and help them until the Lord gives them rest too. Only then may they return to settle their own territory. Their individual blessing does not release them from responsibility to the community. The people of God are one people, not a collection of individuals each pursuing their own portion.
elements.questionHint: Look at what must happen before the eastern tribes may go home in vv18–20.
elements.mainPoint: God’s blessing to one tribe carries **responsibility for the rest**, because they are one people.

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup>Moreover, at that time I pleaded with the Lord, <sup>24</sup>“O, Lord God, you have begun to show me your greatness and strength. (What god in heaven or earth can rival your works and mighty deeds?) <sup>25</sup>Let me please cross over to see the good land on the other side of the Jordan River – this good hill country and the Lebanon!” <sup>26</sup>But the Lord was angry at me because of you and would not listen to me. Instead, he said to me, “Enough of that! Do not speak to me anymore about this matter. <sup>27</sup>Go up to the top of Pisgah and take a good look to the west, north, south, and east, for you will not be allowed to cross the Jordan. <sup>28</sup>Commission Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, because he will lead these people over and will enable them to inherit the land you will see.” <sup>29</sup>So we settled down in the valley opposite Beth Peor.

elements.question: What is the mood at the end of chapter 3, and what does Moses’ exclusion from the land add to his sermon?
elements.sampleAnswer: The mood is both hopeful and sombre. There is encouragement: Joshua will lead the people, God will fight for them, and the victories over Sihon and Og are a down payment on what is to come. But Moses, the greatest leader Israel had known, will see the land from Pisgah and not enter it, and his prayer is refused. He says this is on the people’s account, so their rebellion has cost even their leader his inheritance. That gives the sermon weight: the stakes and the consequences of disobedience are real.
elements.questionHint: Notice Moses’ prayer in vv23–25, God’s answer in vv26–28, and the words ‘on your account’ in v26.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Moses bears a consequence that is at least partly rooted in the people’s failure, not only his own. This is a pattern that recurs in the Bible — the leader who suffers for his people. Without jumping ahead, can you think of where this pattern leads? What does it point toward?

elements.mainPoint: Moses sees the land but **may not enter it**, which shows what the people’s rebellion cost and gives urgency to his sermon.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup>You were not willing to go up, however, but instead rebelled against the Lord your God. <sup>27</sup>You complained among yourselves privately and said, “Because the Lord hates us he brought us from Egypt to deliver us over to the Amorites so they could destroy us! <sup>28</sup>What is going to happen to us? Our brothers have drained away our courage by describing people who are more numerous and taller than we are, and great cities whose defenses appear to be as high as heaven itself! Moreover, they said they saw Anakites there.” <sup>29</sup>So I responded to you, “Do not be terrified of them! <sup>30</sup>The Lord your God is about to go ahead of you; he will fight for you, just as you saw him do in Egypt <sup>31</sup>and in the desert, where you saw him carrying you along like a man carries his son. This he did everywhere you went until you came to this very place.” <sup>32</sup>However, through all this you did not have confidence in the Lord your God, <sup>33</sup>the one who was constantly going before you to find places for you to set up camp. He appeared by fire at night and cloud by day, to show you the way you ought to go.

elements.question: Can you think of ways in which we as Christians might be tempted to disobey God because of fear, doubt or presumption, as the people were in Deuteronomy 1:26–33? Try to be specific.
elements.questionHint: Think of an area where you sense a call or challenge you have been resisting, and ask whether fear, doubt or presumption best describes your response.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>All along the way I, the Lord your God, have blessed your every effort. I have been attentive to your travels through this great wasteland. These forty years I have been with you; you have lacked for nothing.

elements.question: What promises of the Lord are you currently struggling to believe? How does Moses’ reminder in Deuteronomy 2:7 of God’s power and faithfulness help?
elements.questionHint: Ask what evidence of God’s faithfulness, in your life or in others’, you could set against the promise you find hardest to believe.

elements.passageText: <sup>37</sup>As for me, the Lord was also angry with me on your account. He said, “You also will not be able to go there. <sup>38</sup>However, Joshua son of Nun, your assistant, will go. Encourage him, because he will enable Israel to inherit the land.”

elements.question: Moses will not enter the land, and the people are pointed to Joshua as their new leader (Deuteronomy 1:37–38). What does this show about the limits of even the best human leader, and why does that matter when you face your own moments of decision and fear?
elements.questionHint: Notice who may not enter in v37 and who is to lead the people in v38.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Read Hebrews 3:1-6. How does the writer of Hebrews understand the relationship between Moses and Jesus? What specifically is Jesus able to do that Moses could not?

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 4:1-43: The Lord Alone is God

elements.text: Moses has told the story of Israel’s rebellion and God’s faithfulness. Now he draws the conclusion. Chapter 4 is the climax of his first sermon — a great appeal to the people standing before him: given everything you have seen and heard, there is only one rational response. Listen to the Lord. Worship him alone.
As you read, notice the threefold warning structure that runs through the chapter, and the kind of God that makes that warning both urgent and hopeful.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
1Now, Israel, pay attention to the statutes and ordinances I am about to teach you, so that you might live and go on to enter and take possession of the land that the Lord, the God of your ancestors, is giving you. 2Do not add a thing to what I command you nor subtract from it, so that you may keep the commandments of the Lord your God that I am delivering to you. 3You have witnessed what the Lord did at Baal Peor, how he eradicated from your midst everyone who followed Baal Peor. 4But you who remained faithful to the Lord your God are still alive to this very day, every one of you. 5Look! I have taught you statutes and ordinances just as the Lord my God told me to do, so that you might carry them out in the land you are about to enter and possess. 6So be sure to do them, because this will testify of your wise understanding to the people who will learn of all these statutes and say, “Indeed, this great nation is a very wise people.” 7In fact, what other great nation has a god so near to them like the Lord our God whenever we call on him? 8And what other great nation has statutes and ordinances as just as this whole law that I am about to share with you today?

9Again, however, pay very careful attention, lest you forget the things you have seen and disregard them for the rest of your life; instead teach them to your children and grandchildren. 10You stood before the Lord your God at Horeb and he said to me, “Assemble the people before me so that I can tell them my commands. Then they will learn to revere me all the days they live in the land, and they will instruct their children.” 11You approached and stood at the foot of the mountain, a mountain ablaze to the sky above it and yet dark with a thick cloud. 12Then the Lord spoke to you from the middle of the fire; you heard speech but you could not see anything—only a voice was heard. 13And he revealed to you the covenant he has commanded you to keep, the Ten Commandments, writing them on two stone tablets. 14Moreover, at that same time the Lord commanded me to teach you statutes and ordinances for you to keep in the land that you are about to enter and possess.

15Be very careful, then, because you saw no form at the time the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the middle of the fire. 16I say this so you will not corrupt yourselves by making an image in the form of any kind of figure. This includes the likeness of a human male or female, 17any kind of land animal, any bird that flies in the sky, 18anything that crawls on the ground, or any fish in the deep waters under the earth. 19When you look up to the sky and see the sun, moon, and stars—the whole heavenly creation —you must not be seduced to worship and serve them, for the Lord your God has assigned them to all the people of the world. 20You, however, the Lord has selected and brought from Egypt, that iron-smelting furnace, to be his special people as you are today. 21But the Lord became angry with me because of you and vowed that I would never cross the Jordan nor enter the good land that he is about to give you. 22So I must die here in this land; I will not cross the Jordan. But you are going over and will possess that good land. 23Be on guard so that you do not forget the covenant of the Lord your God that he has made with you, and that you do not make an image of any kind, just as he has forbidden you. 24For the Lord your God is a consuming fire; he is a jealous God.

25After you have produced children and grandchildren and have been in the land a long time, if you become corrupt and make an image of any kind and do other evil things before the Lord your God that enrage him, 26I invoke heaven and earth as witnesses against you today that you will surely and swiftly be removed from the very land you are about to cross the Jordan to possess. You will not last long there because you will surely be annihilated. 27Then the Lord will scatter you among the peoples and there will be very few of you among the nations where the Lord will drive you. 28There you will worship gods made by human hands—wood and stone that can neither see, hear, eat, nor smell. 29But if you seek the Lord your God from there, you will find him, if, indeed, you seek him with all your heart and soul. 30In your distress when all these things happen to you in future days, if you return to the Lord your God and obey him 31(for he is a merciful God), he will not let you down or destroy you, for he cannot forget the covenant with your ancestors that he confirmed by oath to them.

32Indeed, ask about the distant past, starting from the day God created humankind on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether there has ever been such a great thing as this, or even a rumor of it. 33Have a people ever heard the voice of God speaking from the middle of fire, as you yourselves have, and lived to tell about it? 34Or has God ever before tried to deliver a nation from the middle of another nation, accompanied by judgments, signs, wonders, war, strength, power, and other very terrifying things like the Lord your God did for you in Egypt before your very eyes? 35You have been taught that the Lord alone is God—there is no other besides him. 36From heaven he spoke to you in order to teach you, and on earth he showed you his great fire from which you also heard his words. 37Moreover, because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants who followed them and personally brought you out of Egypt with his great power 38to dispossess nations greater and stronger than you and brought you here this day to give you their land as your property. 39Today realize and carefully consider that the Lord is God in heaven above and on earth below—there is no other! 40Keep his statutes and commandments that I am setting forth today so that it may go well with you and your descendants and that you may enjoy longevity in the land that the Lord your God is about to give you as a permanent possession.”

41Then Moses selected three cities in the Transjordan, toward the east. 42Anyone who accidentally killed someone without hating him at the time of the accident could flee to one of those cities and be safe. 43These cities are Bezer, in the wilderness plateau, for the Reubenites; Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan for the Manassehites.

elements.question: Before looking at the details, what is the overall impression chapter 4 makes? What is Moses most urgently trying to get his listeners to do?

elements.text: 4:1-8: The Lord Makes His People Unique — So Listen to Him

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>"Now, Israel, pay attention to the statutes and ordinances I am about to teach you, so that you might live and go on to enter and take possession of the land that the Lord, the God of your ancestors, is giving you. <sup>2</sup>Do not add a thing to what I command you nor subtract from it, so that you may keep the commandments of the Lord your God that I am delivering to you. <sup>3</sup>You have witnessed what the Lord did at Baal Peor, how he eradicated from your midst everyone who followed Baal Peor. <sup>4</sup>But you who remained faithful to the Lord your God are still alive today, every one of you. <sup>5</sup>Look! I have taught you statutes and ordinances just as the Lord my God told me to do, so that you might carry them out in the land you are about to enter and possess. <sup>6</sup>So be careful to do them, because this will testify of your wisdom and understanding to the nations who will learn of all these statutes and say, ‘Indeed, this great nation is a very wise people.’ <sup>7</sup>In fact, what other great nation has a god so near to them like the Lord our God whenever we call on him? <sup>8</sup>And what other great nation has statutes and ordinances as just as this whole law that I am about to give you today?

elements.question: What reasons does Moses give in vv1–8 for hearing and keeping the Lord’s decrees?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses gives three reasons. Obedience is the path to life and to possessing the land (v1). The people saw what happened at Baal Peor: those who followed the idol were destroyed, while those who held fast to the Lord are alive (vv3–4). And keeping the law will show the nations a wise and understanding people with a God who is near and laws that are just (vv6–8). Obedience is therefore not arbitrary compliance but a response to something unique.
elements.questionHint: Look for three kinds of reason: what obedience brings (v1), what happened at Baal Peor (vv3–4), and what the nations will see (vv6–8).
elements.mainPoint: Moses gives **three reasons to obey**: it brings life, Baal Peor proves it, and it shows the nations what a people with a near God and a just law look like.

elements.question: What makes Israel unique, according to vv7–8?
elements.sampleAnswer: Israel is set apart by two things: a God who is near whenever they call on him, and a body of law that is perfectly just. Both are put as rhetorical questions that expect the answer that no other nation has anything like them. Their God is not distant or silent; he speaks and answers. Israel’s distinctiveness comes entirely from who God is and what he has given, not from Israel’s size, power or virtue.
elements.questionHint: Look at what the two rhetorical questions in vv7–8 say no other nation has.
elements.mainPoint: Israel is unique not through its own greatness but because **its God is near and his law is just**.

elements.text: 4:9-24: Three Warnings — Remember, Do Not Make Images, Do Not Forget the Covenant

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>Again, however, pay very careful attention, lest you forget the things you have seen and disregard them for the rest of your life; instead teach them to your children and grandchildren. <sup>10</sup>You stood before the Lord your God at Horeb and he said to me, “Assemble the people before me so that I can tell them my commands. Then they will learn to revere me all the days they live in the land, and they will instruct their children.” <sup>11</sup>You approached and stood at the foot of the mountain, a mountain ablaze to the sky above it and yet dark with a thick cloud. <sup>12</sup>Then the Lord spoke to you from the middle of the fire; you heard speech but you could not see anything – only a voice was heard. <sup>13</sup>And he revealed to you the covenant he has commanded you to keep, the ten commandments, writing them on two stone tablets. <sup>14</sup>Moreover, at that same time the Lord commanded me to teach you statutes and ordinances for you to keep in the land which you are about to enter and possess.

elements.question: What does Moses warn the people not to forget about Horeb (vv9–14), and why does he stress that they saw no form (v12)?
elements.sampleAnswer: The first warning (v9) is to take care not to forget what they saw at Horeb, and to teach it to their children. They saw fire, cloud and darkness, but they heard only a voice and saw no form (v12). That contrast shows how God chose to make himself known: through his word, not through an image. He spoke his covenant, the Ten Commandments, for them to hear and obey, and that prepares for the ban on images that follows.
elements.questionHint: Compare what the people saw and what they heard in vv11–12.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Moses says in v9 that the danger is that things will ‘slip from your mind.’ He then commands them to teach these things to their children and grandchildren. What does this suggest about the nature of spiritual memory — is it automatic, or does it require deliberate effort? What practices sustain it?

elements.mainPoint: God made himself known at Horeb by **a voice, not a form**: a word to obey, not an image to look at.

elements.passageText: <sup>15</sup>Be very careful, then, because you saw no form at the time the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the middle of the fire. <sup>16</sup>I say this so you will not corrupt yourselves by making an image in the form of any kind of figure. This includes the likeness of a human male or female, <sup>17</sup>any kind of land animal, any bird that flies in the sky, <sup>18</sup>anything that crawls on the ground, or any fish in the deep waters of the earth. <sup>19</sup>When you look up to the sky and see the sun, moon, and stars – the whole heavenly creation – you must not be seduced to worship and serve them, for the Lord your God has assigned them to all the people of the world. <sup>20</sup>You, however, the Lord has selected and brought from Egypt, that iron-smelting furnace, to be his special people as you are today. <sup>21</sup>But the Lord became angry with me because of you and vowed that I would never cross the Jordan nor enter the good land that he is about to give you. <sup>22</sup>So I must die here in this land; I will not cross the Jordan. But you are going over and will possess that good land. <sup>23</sup>Be on guard so that you do not forget the covenant of the Lord your God that he has made with you, and that you do not make an image of any kind, just as he has forbidden you. <sup>24</sup>For the Lord your God is a consuming fire; he is a jealous God.

elements.question: What is the second warning (vv15–18), and why is making an image of God so serious even if the motive is sincere?
elements.sampleAnswer: The second warning is not to make any carved image of any kind. Moses roots it in Horeb: because they saw no form when the Lord spoke from the fire, they must not make one. An image is something humans make and control, while the living God speaks and cannot be managed. Even sincere image-making would swap the Creator’s self-revelation for human invention. God is a consuming fire and a jealous God (v24), a faithful covenant God who will not share what belongs to the relationship.
elements.questionHint: Notice the reason Moses gives in v15 and what he says God is like in v24.
elements.mainPoint: Because God showed no form at Horeb, **any image of him misrepresents him**, however sincere the worship.

elements.text: 4:25-40: Even When You Fail, He Will Remember

elements.passageText: <sup>25</sup>After you have produced children and grandchildren and have been in the land a long time, if you become corrupt and make an image of any kind and do other evil things before the Lord your God that enrage him, <sup>26</sup>I invoke heaven and earth as witnesses against you today that you will surely and swiftly be removed from the very land you are about to cross the Jordan to possess. You will not last long there because you will surely be annihilated. <sup>27</sup>Then the Lord will scatter you among the peoples and there will be very few of you among the nations where the Lord will drive you. <sup>28</sup>There you will worship gods made by human hands – wood and stone that can neither see, hear, eat, nor smell. <sup>29</sup>But if you seek the Lord your God from there, you will find him, if, indeed, you seek him with all your heart and soul. <sup>30</sup>In your distress when all these things happen to you in the latter days, if you return to the Lord your God and obey him <sup>31</sup>(for he is a merciful God), he will not let you down or destroy you, for he cannot forget the covenant with your ancestors that he confirmed by oath to them.

elements.question: What does Moses warn will happen if the people turn to idols (vv25–28), and what hope breaks through in vv29–31?
elements.sampleAnswer: If they forget and make idols, they will be driven from the land and scattered among the nations, serving gods of wood and stone that cannot see, hear, eat or smell. Yet even from exile, if they seek the Lord with all their heart and soul, they will find him. The hope rests on God’s character: he is merciful and will not forget the covenant he swore to their ancestors. The tenderness of vv29–31 inside a warning of judgment shows he does not lock the door behind those who leave.
elements.questionHint: Notice what the people must do in v29 and what the Lord is called in v31.
elements.mainPoint: Idolatry leads to exile, but **the way back stays open** because the Lord is merciful and keeps his covenant.

elements.passageText: <sup>32</sup>Indeed, ask about the distant past, starting from the day God created humankind on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether there has ever been such a great thing as this, or even a rumor of it. <sup>33</sup>Have a people ever heard the voice of God speaking from the middle of fire, as you yourselves have, and lived to tell about it? <sup>34</sup>Or has God ever before tried to deliver a nation from the middle of another nation, accompanied by judgments, signs, wonders, war, strength, power, and other very terrifying things like the Lord your God did for you in Egypt before your very eyes? <sup>35</sup>You have been taught that the Lord alone is God – there is no other besides him. <sup>36</sup>From heaven he spoke to you in order to teach you, and on earth he showed you his great fire from which you also heard his words. <sup>37</sup>Moreover, because he loved your ancestors, he chose their descendants who followed them and personally brought you out of Egypt with his great power <sup>38</sup>to dispossess nations greater and stronger than you and brought you here this day to give you their land as your property. <sup>39</sup>Today realize and carefully consider that the Lord is God in heaven above and on earth below – there is no other! <sup>40</sup>Keep his statutes and commandments that I am setting forth today so that it may go well with you and your descendants and that you may enjoy longevity in the land that the Lord your God is about to give you as a permanent possession.

elements.question: What has the Lord done that no other god has done (vv32–38), and what conclusion does Moses draw in v39?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses asks whether any people has ever heard a god speak from the fire and lived, or whether any god has taken one nation out of another by signs, wonders and war. The answer is no. The Lord spoke at Horeb and rescued Israel from Egypt, acting in history because he loved their ancestors and chose their descendants (v37). So Moses concludes that the Lord is God in heaven above and on earth below, and that there is no other (v39).
elements.questionHint: Notice the two events in vv33–34 and the reason given for them in v37.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Moses ends this section with a series of rhetorical questions that are designed to be unanswerable: no other god has done what the Lord has done. How does this argument work — and could a similar argument be made today, starting not just from the exodus but from the cross and resurrection? What would that look like?

elements.mainPoint: The Lord’s speaking at Horeb and rescue from Egypt prove his claim: **he alone is God**, in heaven and on earth.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>9</sup>Again, however, pay very careful attention, lest you forget the things you have seen and disregard them for the rest of your life; instead teach them to your children and grandchildren.

elements.question: Moses warns that what they have seen and heard can fade from their minds unless they remember it and pass it on (Deuteronomy 4:9). How can we be tempted to drift from God’s word, and what habits or practices help us resist that drift?
elements.questionHint: Name one way you have drifted from God’s word and one habit that would help you hold on to it.

elements.passageText: <sup>39</sup>Today realize and carefully consider that the Lord is God in heaven above and on earth below – there is no other!

elements.question: What idolatry is most likely to tempt us as Christians today? How does Deuteronomy 4:39 help us see the seriousness of it, and the way out?
elements.questionHint: Think of one area of life where you give the Lord least say, and ask what acknowledging him there would mean.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 4:44-5:33: Walk in the Way the Lord Your God Has Commanded

elements.text: Moses’ first sermon has ended. Now begins the second — and it is the heart of the book. Moses takes the new generation back to Horeb, back to the moment when God spoke from fire and gave his people the Ten Commandments. But he is not simply recalling history. He is insisting that this covenant is theirs — personally, directly, today.
As you read, pay attention to the frame around the commandments — who gave them, to whom, through what means, and for what purpose. The frame changes how you read everything inside it.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
44This is the law that Moses set before the Israelites. 45These are the stipulations, statutes, and ordinances that Moses spoke to the Israelites after he had brought them out of Egypt, 46in the Transjordan, in the valley opposite Beth Peor, in the land of King Sihon of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. (It is he whom Moses and the Israelites attacked after they came out of Egypt. 47They possessed his land and that of King Og of Bashan—both of whom were Amorite kings in the Transjordan, to the east. 48Their territory extended from Aroer at the edge of the Arnon valley as far as Mount Siyon —that is, Hermon— 49including all the rift valley of the Transjordan in the east to the sea of the rift valley, beneath the slopes of Pisgah.)

5:1Then Moses called all the people of Israel together and said to them: “Listen, Israel, to the statutes and ordinances that I am about to deliver to you today; learn them and be careful to keep them! 2The Lord our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. 3He did not make this covenant with our ancestors but with us, we who are here today, all of us living now. 4The Lord spoke face to face with you at the mountain, from the middle of the fire. 5(I was standing between the Lord and you at that time to reveal the Lord’s message to you, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain.) He said:

6“I am the Lord your God—he who brought you from the land of Egypt, from the place of slavery.

7“You must not have any other gods besides me.

8“You must not make for yourself an image of anything in heaven above, on earth below, or in the waters beneath. 9You must not worship or serve them, for I, the Lord your God, am a jealous God. I punish the sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons for the sin of the fathers who reject me, 10but I show covenant faithfulness to the thousands who choose me and keep my commandments.

11“You must not make use of the name of the Lord your God for worthless purposes, for the Lord will not exonerate anyone who abuses his name that way.

12“Be careful to observe the Sabbath day just as the Lord your God has commanded you. 13You are to work and do all your tasks in six days, 14but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. On that day you must not do any work, you, your son, your daughter, your male slave, your female slave, your ox, your donkey, any other animal, or the resident foreigner who lives with you, so that your male and female slaves, like yourself, may have rest. 15Recall that you were slaves in the land of Egypt and that the Lord your God brought you out of there by strength and power. That is why the Lord your God has commanded you to observe the Sabbath day.

16“Honor your father and your mother just as the Lord your God has commanded you to do, so that your days may be extended and that it may go well with you in the land that he is about to give you.

17“You must not murder.

18“You must not commit adultery.

19“You must not steal.

20“You must not offer false testimony against another. 21You must not desire another man’s wife, nor should you crave his house, his field, his male and female servants, his ox, his donkey, or anything else he owns.”

22The Lord said these things to your entire assembly at the mountain from the middle of the fire, the cloud, and the darkness with a loud voice, and that was all he said. Then he inscribed the words on two stone tablets and gave them to me. 23Then, when you heard the voice from the midst of the darkness while the mountain was ablaze, all your tribal leaders and elders approached me. 24You said, “The Lord our God has shown us his great glory, and we have heard him speak from the middle of the fire. It is now clear to us that God can speak to human beings and they can keep on living. 25But now, why should we die, because this intense fire will consume us? If we keep hearing the voice of the Lord our God we will die! 26Who is there from the entire human race who has heard the voice of the living God speaking from the middle of the fire as we have, and has lived? 27You go near so that you can hear everything the Lord our God is saying and then you can tell us whatever he says to you; then we will pay attention and do it.” 28When the Lord heard you speaking to me, he said to me, “I have heard what these people have said to you—they have spoken well. 29If only it would really be their desire to fear me and obey all my commandments in the future, so that it may go well with them and their descendants forever. 30Go and tell them, ‘Return to your tents!’ 31But as for you, remain here with me so I can declare to you all the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that you are to teach them, so that they can carry them out in the land I am about to give them.” 32Be careful, therefore, to do exactly what the Lord your God has commanded you; do not turn right or left! 33Walk just as he has commanded you so that you may live, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land you are going to possess.

elements.question: Before working through the details, what strikes you about the context in which the Ten Commandments are given here? What do you notice about the order in which things happen?

elements.text: 4:44-5:5: The Context of the Commandments

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses called all the Israelites together and said to them: "Listen, Israel, to the statutes and ordinances I am about to deliver to you today; learn them and be careful to keep them. <sup>2</sup>The Lord our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. <sup>3</sup>He did not make this covenant with our ancestors but with us -- we, all of us who are alive today. <sup>4</sup>The Lord spoke to you face to face at the mountain, from the middle of the fire. <sup>5</sup>(I was standing between the Lord and you at that time to tell you the word of the Lord, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain.) He said:

elements.question: Why does Moses say in v3 that the covenant was made with ‘us’ and not with ‘our ancestors’, when most of his audience were children or unborn at Horeb?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses will not let his hearers treat the covenant as something that happened to their parents. Most of those at Horeb had died and the people before him were born in the wilderness, yet he says the covenant was made with ‘us’. This is a claim about their standing before God, not about chronology. The covenant is a living relationship that each generation enters directly, so no one can watch obedience from a safe distance.
elements.questionHint: Notice who Moses says the covenant was made with, and which generation he is addressing.
elements.mainPoint: The covenant is **not an inheritance to admire from a distance** but a relationship each generation is personally in.

elements.question: Moses says in v5 that he stood between the Lord and the people because they were afraid. What does this tell us about the problem of approaching a holy God?
elements.sampleAnswer: The people’s fear was a right instinct, not cowardice: a holy God speaking directly to sinful people is dangerous, and the fire on the mountain expresses that holiness. They needed someone to stand between them and God. Moses did this, standing where they could not, receiving the word and bringing it to them. It shows the human problem: sin has opened a gap between us and a holy God that we cannot bridge ourselves.
elements.questionHint: Notice why the people could not go up the mountain, according to v5.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Read 1 Timothy 2:5 and Hebrews 1:1-2. How does the New Testament understand what Moses was doing when he ‘stood between the Lord and the people’? What does Jesus do that Moses could not?

elements.mainPoint: Sinful people cannot approach a holy God directly; **they need a mediator**, a role Moses fills here.

elements.text: 5:6-21: The Ten Commandments

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>“I am the Lord your God, he who brought you from the land of Egypt, from the place of slavery.

elements.question: What does it show that God reminds Israel of the exodus (v6) before giving a single commandment?
elements.sampleAnswer: The order matters. God does not say ‘keep these commandments and I will rescue you’; he reminds them that he has already brought them out of slavery. The commandments come after the rescue, so they are not terms to earn his favour but the shape of life for people already redeemed. Obedience is meant to flow from gratitude, not from an attempt to win acceptance. It is the same pattern as the gospel: grace first, then a life that responds.
elements.questionHint: Notice the order in v6: what God has already done, then what he commands.
elements.mainPoint: **Redemption comes before law**: God’s commands are the shape of life for people he has already rescued.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>‘You must not have any other gods besides me. <sup>8</sup>You must not make for yourself an image of anything in heaven above, on earth below, or in the waters beneath. <sup>9</sup>You must not worship or serve them, for I, the Lord your God, am a jealous God. I punish the sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons for the sin of the fathers who reject me, <sup>10</sup>but I show covenant faithfulness to the thousands who choose me and keep my commandments. <sup>11</sup>You must not make use of the name of the Lord your God for worthless purposes, for the Lord will not exonerate anyone who abuses his name that way. <sup>12</sup>Be careful to observe the Sabbath day just as the Lord your God has commanded you. <sup>13</sup>You are to work and do all your tasks in six days, <sup>14</sup>but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. On that day you must not do any work, you, your son, your daughter, your male slave, your female slave, your ox, your donkey, any other animal, or the foreigner who lives with you, so that your male and female slaves, like yourself, may have rest. <sup>15</sup>Recall that you were slaves in the land of Egypt and that the Lord your God brought you out of there by strength and power. That is why the Lord your God has commanded you to observe the Sabbath day. <sup>16</sup>Honor your father and your mother just as the Lord your God has commanded you to do, so that your days may be extended and that it may go well with you in the land that he is about to give you. <sup>17</sup>You must not murder. <sup>18</sup>You must not commit adultery. <sup>19</sup>You must not steal. <sup>20</sup>You must not offer false testimony against another. <sup>21</sup>You must not desire another man’s wife, nor should you crave his house, his field, his male and female servants, his ox, his donkey, or anything else he owns.”

elements.question: What is being protected by the Ten Commandments in vv7–21, and what would positive obedience look like?
elements.sampleAnswer: The first commandments protect God’s uniqueness and the honour of his name; positive obedience means treating the Lord as the only source of security and worth and speaking of him with truth and reverence. The Sabbath protects rest and freedom, grounded here in the memory of slavery, so free people rest and let others rest. Honouring parents protects the family and the passing on of wisdom. The commands on murder, adultery, theft and false witness protect life, marriage, property and truth. The last, against coveting, reaches the heart, since desire drives most other sin.
elements.questionHint: Take the commandments in groups, those about God (vv7–15) and those about neighbours (vv16–21), and ask what each group guards.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Notice that the Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy (v15) is grounded in the memory of slavery in Egypt, whereas in Exodus 20:11 it is grounded in creation. What does each grounding add to our understanding of the Sabbath? How might Hebrews 4 help us think about what Sabbath rest means for Christians?

elements.mainPoint: The commandments **guard what is most precious**: God’s uniqueness, rest and freedom, the family, and the life, marriage, property and truth of our neighbours.

elements.text: 5:22-33: The Mediator and the Purpose of the Commands

elements.passageText: <sup>23</sup>Then, when you heard the voice from the midst of the darkness while the mountain was ablaze, all your tribal leaders and elders approached me. <sup>24</sup>You said, “The Lord our God has shown us his great glory and we have heard him speak from the middle of the fire. It is now clear to us that God can speak to human beings and they can keep on living. <sup>25</sup>But now, why should we die, because this intense fire will consume us! If we keep hearing the voice of the Lord our God we will die! <sup>26</sup>Who is there from the entire human race who has heard the voice of the living God speaking from the middle of the fire as we have, and has lived? <sup>27</sup>You go near so that you can hear everything the Lord our God is saying and then you can tell us whatever he says to you; then we will pay attention and do it.” <sup>28</sup>When the Lord heard you speaking to me, he said to me, “I have heard what these people have said to you – they have spoken well. <sup>29</sup>If only it would really be their desire to fear me and obey all my commandments in the future, so that it may go well with them and their descendants forever. <sup>30</sup>Go and tell them, ‘Return to your tents!’ <sup>31</sup>But as for you, remain here with me so I can declare to you all the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that you are to teach them, so that they can carry them out in the land I am about to give them.” <sup>32</sup>Be careful, therefore, to do exactly what the Lord your God has commanded you; do not turn right or left! <sup>33</sup>Walk just as he has commanded you so that you may live, that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land you are going to possess.

elements.question: How do the people respond to the voice of the Lord in vv23–27, and what does God’s wish in v29 reveal about their problem?
elements.sampleAnswer: The people are terrified that the fire will consume them if they keep hearing the living God, so they ask Moses to go near and listen for them. God says they have spoken well (v28), so their need of a mediator is a proper response. But his wish in v29 is full of longing: if only they would fear him and keep his commandments always. Their reverence in the moment will not match their long-term obedience, and that gap is what the rest of Deuteronomy addresses.
elements.questionHint: Compare what God commends in v28 with what he longs for in v29.
elements.mainPoint: The people rightly fear God and ask for a mediator, but **God longs for fear that lasts as obedience**.

elements.question: What do vv32–33 tell us about the purpose of God’s commands?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses sums up the purpose of the commands: walk in all the ways the Lord has commanded, so that they may live and that it may go well with them in the land. The goal is life, full and lasting, not a list of burdens. The image of walking one way shows obedience as a whole manner of life, a path that leads somewhere. God’s commandments show his people the route to the life he intends for them.
elements.questionHint: Notice the image Moses uses for obedience and the results he promises in v33.
elements.mainPoint: The commands are **a path to life**, not a burden to endure.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>“I am the Lord your God, he who brought you from the land of Egypt, from the place of slavery.

elements.question: God grounds all the commandments in his act of redemption (v6). How does understanding this order — redemption before law — change how we relate to the commandments? What does it feel like to obey from gratitude rather than from obligation?
elements.questionHint: Think of the difference between something you do from gratitude and something you do from obligation, and ask which v6 invites.

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>Be careful to observe the Sabbath day just as the Lord your God has commanded you. <sup>13</sup>You are to work and do all your tasks in six days, <sup>14</sup>but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. On that day you must not do any work, you, your son, your daughter, your male slave, your female slave, your ox, your donkey, any other animal, or the foreigner who lives with you, so that your male and female slaves, like yourself, may have rest. <sup>15</sup>Recall that you were slaves in the land of Egypt and that the Lord your God brought you out of there by strength and power. That is why the Lord your God has commanded you to observe the Sabbath day.

elements.question: The Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy 5:12–15 is grounded in the memory of slavery: free people get to rest. What might it look like for us to practise Sabbath, not as a legalistic rule but as an embodied declaration that we are not slaves to productivity, achievement or the fear of falling behind?
elements.questionHint: Ask what your difficulty in stopping shows about what you are trusting in.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 6: Love the Loving Lord with Everything

elements.text: If the Ten Commandments are the body of Moses’ second sermon, chapter 6 gives them their heart. Moses has told the people what God requires; now he tells them the spirit from which all of that must flow. It is not a list of rules but a relationship — a call to love the Lord with every part of who they are.
As you read, notice what Moses predicts will threaten that love — and what he says must be done to sustain it.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
1Now these are the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that the Lord your God instructed me to teach you so that you may carry them out in the land where you are headed 2and that you may so revere the Lord your God that you will keep all his statutes and commandments that I am giving you—you, your children, and your grandchildren—all your lives, to prolong your days. 3Pay attention, Israel, and be careful to do this so that it may go well with you and that you may increase greatly in number —as the Lord, the God of your ancestors, said to you, you will have a land flowing with milk and honey.

4Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord is one! 5You must love the Lord your God with your whole mind, your whole being, and all your strength.

6These words I am commanding you today must be kept in mind, 7and you must teach them to your children and speak of them as you sit in your house, as you walk along the road, as you lie down, and as you get up. 8You should tie them as a reminder on your forearm and fasten them as symbols on your forehead. 9Inscribe them on the doorframes of your houses and gates.

10Then when the Lord your God brings you to the land he promised your ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give you—a land with large, fine cities you did not build, 11houses filled with choice things you did not accumulate, hewn-out cisterns you did not dig, and vineyards and olive groves you did not plant—and you eat your fill, 12be careful not to forget the Lord who brought you out of Egypt, that place of slavery. 13You must revere the Lord your God, serve him, and take oaths using only his name. 14You must not go after other gods, those of the surrounding peoples, 15for the Lord your God, who is present among you, is a jealous God—his anger will erupt against you and remove you from the land.

16You must not put the Lord your God to the test as you did at Massah. 17Keep his commandments very carefully, as well as the stipulations and statutes he commanded you to observe. 18Do whatever is proper and good before the Lord so that it may go well with you and that you may enter and occupy the good land that he promised your ancestors, 19and that you may drive out all your enemies just as the Lord said.

20When your children ask you later on, “What are the stipulations, statutes, and ordinances that the Lord our God commanded you?” 21you must say to them, “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt, but the Lord brought us out of Egypt in a powerful way. 22And he brought signs and great, devastating wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on his whole family before our very eyes. 23He delivered us from there so that he could give us the land he had promised our ancestors. 24The Lord commanded us to obey all these statutes and to revere him so that it may always go well for us and he may preserve us, as he has to this day. 25We will be innocent if we carefully keep all these commandments before the Lord our God, just as he demands.”

elements.question: The Shema — ‘The Lord our God, the Lord is one’ — is the central confession of Jewish faith, recited twice daily to this day. Before looking at the details, what impression does it make on you that the entire call of the chapter flows from this single declaration?

elements.text: 6:1-9: Love the Lord Your God with Everything

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord is one! <sup>5</sup>You must love the Lord your God with your whole mind, your whole being, and all your strength. <sup>6</sup>These words I am commanding you today must be kept in mind, <sup>7</sup>and you must teach them to your children and speak of them as you sit in your house, as you walk along the road, as you lie down, and as you get up. <sup>8</sup>You should tie them as a reminder on your forearm and fasten them as symbols on your forehead. <sup>9</sup>Inscribe them on the doorframes of your houses and gates.

elements.question: What does v4 say about the Lord, and why does that lead to the command in v5 to love him with everything?
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 4 declares that the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. He is unique and undivided: not one option among competitors and not a partial truth alongside others. Because God is one, the response to him must be undivided, and fractional allegiance to the one God is a contradiction. The three phrases of v5 (whole mind, whole being, all your strength) cover every dimension of a person, so the point is totality, not three separate parts. The comprehensiveness of the demand follows from the comprehensiveness of who God is.
elements.questionHint: Ask why the oneness of God calls for total love rather than just sincere love.
elements.mainPoint: Because the Lord is one, **the love he asks for is undivided**: the whole person, with nothing held back.

elements.question: How do vv6–9 relate to the command to love God in v5, and what kind of love do they describe?
elements.sampleAnswer: The instructions in vv6–9 answer the question of what loving God with everything looks like day to day. Moses says to keep his words in mind, teach them to the children, talk about them at home and on the road, and have them before the eyes and on the doorframes. Love for God is expressed and sustained by keeping his word central to ordinary life. It is not mainly a feeling or a peak experience but a whole-of-life orientation, built up through daily habit and attention to his word.
elements.questionHint: Notice the times and places listed in vv7–9: sitting, walking, lying down, getting up, doorframes and gates.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Read Mark 12:28-34 and notice how Jesus uses these verses. Why does he call this ‘the greatest commandment’? What does it mean for all the other commandments that this one is greatest?

keyTerms: habit|whole of life|orientation|not just a feeling|not primarily a feeling|attentive
elements.mainPoint: Loving God is **shown in daily life**, by keeping his word at the centre of ordinary routines, not only in strong feelings.

elements.text: 6:10-19: Three Things That Will Challenge Your Love

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup>Then when the Lord your God brings you to the land he promised your ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give you – a land with large, fine cities you did not build, <sup>11</sup>houses filled with choice things you did not accumulate, hewn out cisterns you did not dig, and vineyards and olive groves you did not plant – and you eat your fill, <sup>12</sup>be careful not to forget the Lord who brought you out of Egypt, that place of slavery. <sup>13</sup>You must revere the Lord your God, serve him, and take oaths using only his name. <sup>14</sup>You must not go after other gods, those of the surrounding peoples, <sup>15</sup>for the Lord your God, who is present among you, is a jealous God and his anger will erupt against you and remove you from the land. <sup>16</sup>You must not put the Lord your God to the test as you did at Massah. <sup>17</sup>Keep his commandments very carefully, as well as the stipulations and statutes he commanded you to observe. <sup>18</sup>Do whatever is proper and good before the Lord so that it may go well with you and that you may enter and occupy the good land that he promised your ancestors, <sup>19</sup>and that you may drive out all your enemies just as the Lord said.

elements.question: Moses warns of three things that will challenge Israel’s love for the Lord (vv10–19). What are they, and why does he spend most time on the first?
elements.sampleAnswer: The three threats are prosperity (vv10–12), conformity to the gods of the surrounding peoples (vv13–15), and testing the Lord, as at Massah, when hardship comes (v16). Moses gives most attention to prosperity because it is the least expected. We expect hardship to erode faith, but abundance can make God feel unnecessary and quietly switch off our dependence on him. The danger is not dramatic rejection but a slow, comfortable drift into forgetting the one who gave the blessing.
elements.questionHint: Look at vv10–12 for the first, vv13–15 for the second and v16 for the third.
elements.mainPoint: Moses’ chief warning is that **prosperity can make us forget the Lord**, which is more subtle than hardship or rival gods.

elements.text: 6:20-25: Love Him Because He First Loved You
