elements.passageText: <sup>20</sup>When your children ask you later on, “What are the stipulations, statutes, and ordinances that the Lord our God commanded you?” <sup>21</sup>you must say to them, “We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt, but the Lord brought us out of Egypt in a powerful way. <sup>22</sup>And he brought signs and great, devastating wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on his whole family before our very eyes. <sup>23</sup>He delivered us from there so that he could give us the land he had promised our ancestors. <sup>24</sup>The Lord commanded us to obey all these statutes and to revere him so that it may always go well for us and he may preserve us, as he has to this day. <sup>25</sup>We will be innocent if we carefully keep all these commandments before the Lord our God, just as he demands.”

elements.question: When a child asks why God’s commands must be kept, what answer does Moses prescribe (vv20–25), and what does it show about the ground of obedience?
elements.sampleAnswer: The answer begins not with the commands but with what God did: we were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt and the Lord brought us out with a powerful hand. The reason to obey is first of all a story of what God has already done. His rescue is the ground from which love and obedience grow, so Israel’s love is a response to his love, and even the commands are given for their good (v24). Obedience is therefore the fitting response of people who have been loved first, not a burden imposed from outside.
elements.questionHint: Notice where the answer begins in v21: with a commandment or with something else?
elements.mainPoint: We obey because **God rescued us first**; the commands make sense inside a story of grace.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord is one! <sup>5</sup>You must love the Lord your God with your whole mind, your whole being, and all your strength.

elements.question: Moses says love for God is to show up in every part of life — sitting, walking, lying down, getting up. What does it look like to love the Lord with everything in your particular context? Think of both inward and outward expressions.
elements.questionHint: Ask where evidence of a life oriented towards the Lord would be clearest in your daily routine, and where it would be thinnest.

elements.passageText: <sup>10</sup>Then when the Lord your God brings you to the land he promised your ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give you – a land with large, fine cities you did not build, <sup>11</sup>houses filled with choice things you did not accumulate, hewn out cisterns you did not dig, and vineyards and olive groves you did not plant – and you eat your fill, <sup>12</sup>be careful not to forget the Lord who brought you out of Egypt, that place of slavery.

elements.question: How might prosperity, conformity or hardship (Deuteronomy 6:10–12 and the verses that follow) challenge your love for the Lord? What specific form do those threats take in your own life? What can we do to help each other remain faithful?
elements.questionHint: Ask why watching yourself alone is not enough, and what a community can do that self-monitoring cannot.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 7: Do Not Compromise — Live Distinctively as a Holy People

elements.text: Chapter 7 is the first expansion of the Shema’s call to love God with everything. And the first thing that wholehearted love looks like, Moses says, is this: do not compromise. The people God has chosen are set apart for him — and anything that threatens that distinctiveness must be taken with the utmost seriousness.
As you read, notice why Moses takes the threat of compromise so seriously — and where the antidote to fear-driven compromise is found.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
1When the Lord your God brings you to the land that you are going to occupy and forces out many nations before you—Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and powerful than you— 2and he delivers them over to you and you attack them, you must utterly annihilate them. Make no treaty with them and show them no mercy! 3You must not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, 4for they will turn your sons away from me to worship other gods. Then the anger of the Lord will erupt against you and he will quickly destroy you. 5Instead, this is what you must do to them: You must tear down their altars, shatter their sacred pillars, cut down their sacred Asherah poles, and burn up their idols. 6For you are a people holy to the Lord your God. He has chosen you to be his people, prized above all others on the face of the earth.

7It is not because you were more numerous than all the other peoples that the Lord favored and chose you—for in fact you were the least numerous of all peoples. 8Rather it is because of his love for you and his faithfulness to the promise he solemnly vowed to your ancestors that the Lord brought you out with great power, redeeming you from the place of slavery, from the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt. 9So realize that the Lord your God is the true God, the faithful God who keeps covenant faithfully with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, 10but who pays back those who hate him as they deserve and destroys them. He will not ignore those who hate him but will repay them as they deserve! 11So keep the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that I today am commanding you to do.

12If you obey these ordinances and are careful to do them, the Lord your God will faithfully keep covenant with you as he promised your ancestors. 13He will love and bless you, and make you numerous. He will bless you with many children, with the produce of your soil, your grain, your new wine, your olive oil, the offspring of your oxen, and the young of your flocks in the land that he promised your ancestors to give you. 14You will be blessed beyond all peoples; there will be no barrenness among you or your livestock. 15The Lord will protect you from all sickness, and you will not experience any of the terrible diseases that you knew in Egypt; instead he will inflict them on all those who hate you.

16You must destroy all the people whom the Lord your God is about to deliver over to you; you must not pity them or worship their gods, for that will be a snare to you. 17If you think, “These nations are more numerous than I—how can I dispossess them?” 18you must not fear them. You must carefully recall what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and all Egypt, 19the great judgments you saw, the signs and wonders, the strength and power by which he brought you out—thus the Lord your God will do to all the people you fear. 20Furthermore, the Lord your God will release hornets among them until the very last ones who hide from you perish. 21You must not tremble in their presence, for the Lord your God, who is present among you, is a great and awesome God. 22He, the God who leads you, will expel the nations little by little. You will not be allowed to destroy them all at once lest the wild animals overrun you. 23The Lord your God will give them over to you; he will throw them into a great panic until they are destroyed. 24He will hand over their kings to you, and you will erase their very names from memory. Nobody will be able to resist you until you destroy them. 25You must burn the images of their gods, but do not covet the silver and gold that covers them so much that you take it for yourself and thus become ensnared by it; for it is abhorrent to the Lord your God. 26You must not bring any abhorrent thing into your house and thereby become an object of divine wrath along with it. You must absolutely detest and abhor it, for it is an object of divine wrath.

elements.question: Chapter 7 contains some of the most demanding and difficult material in Deuteronomy. Before working through it, what is your first reaction? What questions does it raise for you?

elements.text: 7:1-5: Do Not Compromise

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>When the Lord your God brings you to the land that you are going to occupy and forces out many nations before you – Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and powerful than you – <sup>2</sup>and he delivers them over to you and you attack them, you must utterly annihilate them. Make no treaty with them and show them no mercy! <sup>3</sup>You must not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, <sup>4</sup>for they will turn your sons away from me to worship other gods. Then the anger of the Lord will erupt against you and he will quickly destroy you. <sup>5</sup>Instead, this is what you must do to them: You must tear down their altars, shatter their sacred pillars, cut down their sacred Asherah poles, and burn up their idols. <sup>6</sup>For you are a people holy to the Lord your God. He has chosen you to be his people, prized above all others on the face of the earth.

elements.question: What reason does Moses give in v4 for forbidding covenants and intermarriage with the Canaanite nations, and what does it reveal about idolatry?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses’ reason is that they will turn Israel’s children away from following the Lord to serve other gods. The concern is theological, not ethnic: it comes from a realistic view of how spiritual corruption spreads. Idolatry is contagious and works through relationship and the gradual normalisation of rival loyalties. The command to destroy the altars and pillars in v5 makes the same point: the apparatus of false worship must be removed, not adapted or reused.
elements.questionHint: Look at who is turned away, and by whom, in v4.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: The command to utterly destroy the nations raises serious ethical questions that generations of readers have wrestled with. A few orientation points: this is a unique, historically specific command for a unique moment — it is not a general licence for religious violence. And within Deuteronomy itself, the focus quickly shifts from physical destruction to the destruction of the worship infrastructure (v5). But sit with the discomfort: what does the severity of this command tell you about how seriously God takes the threat of idolatry to his people?

elements.mainPoint: Idolatry spreads **through relationship and influence**, which is why Moses insists on a clean break.

elements.text: 7:6-11: The Lord Chose You

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>For you are a people holy to the Lord your God. He has chosen you to be his people, prized above all others on the face of the earth. <sup>7</sup>It is not because you were more numerous than all the other peoples that the Lord favored and chose you – for in fact you were the least numerous of all peoples. <sup>8</sup>Rather it is because of his love for you and his faithfulness to the promise he solemnly vowed to your ancestors that the Lord brought you out with great power, redeeming you from the place of slavery, from the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt. <sup>9</sup>So realize that the Lord your God is the true God, the faithful God who keeps covenant faithfully with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, <sup>10</sup>but who pays back those who hate him as they deserve and destroys them. He will not ignore those who hate him but will repay them as they deserve! <sup>11</sup>So keep the commandments, statutes, and ordinances that I today am commanding you to do.

elements.question: Why did the Lord choose Israel (vv7–8), and what reason does Moses rule out?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses rules out size, strength and anything that would make Israel a promising choice: they were the fewest of all peoples. The reason lies entirely with God: he loved them and kept the oath he swore to their ancestors. This means Israel’s status can never be a source of pride, because they brought nothing to the relationship. It also grounds the call to be holy in gratitude rather than achievement.
elements.questionHint: Look at what Moses says about Israel’s numbers in v7 and what he gives as the reason in v8.
elements.mainPoint: God chose Israel **not because they were great but because he loved them** and kept his oath.

elements.text: 7:12-26: Trust the Lord and Do Not Fear

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup>If you think, “These nations are more numerous than I – how can I dispossess them?” <sup>18</sup>you must not fear them. You must carefully recall what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and all Egypt, <sup>19</sup>the great judgments you saw, the signs and wonders, the strength and power by which he brought you out – thus the Lord your God will do to all the people you fear. <sup>20</sup>Furthermore, the Lord your God will release hornets among them until the very last ones who hide from you perish. <sup>21</sup>You must not tremble in their presence, for the Lord your God, who is present among you, is a great and awesome God. <sup>22</sup>He, the God who leads you, will expel the nations little by little. You will not be allowed to destroy them all at once lest the wild animals overrun you. <sup>23</sup>The Lord your God will give them over to you; he will throw them into a great panic until they are destroyed. <sup>24</sup>He will hand over their kings to you and you will erase their very names from memory. Nobody will be able to resist you until you destroy them. <sup>25</sup>You must burn the images of their gods, but do not covet the silver and gold that covers them so much that you take it for yourself and thus become ensnared by it; for it is abhorrent to the Lord your God. <sup>26</sup>You must not bring any abhorrent thing into your house and thereby become an object of divine wrath along with it. You must absolutely detest and abhor it, for it is an object of divine wrath.

elements.question: How does Moses answer the people’s fear of stronger nations (vv17–24), and what does this show about faith-based courage?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses does not say the nations are weak; he takes the fear seriously and then widens the view. He tells them to remember what the Lord did to Pharaoh and all Egypt (v18) and that the same Lord will do the same to the peoples they fear. Courage in Deuteronomy rests on evidence, not on pretending the obstacle is small. The Lord is in their midst, a great and awesome God (v21). The conquest will also come bit by bit (v22), so faithfulness has to be sustained over time.
elements.questionHint: Look at what Moses tells them to remember in v18.
elements.mainPoint: Faith-based courage **does not shrink the danger; it remembers what God has already done**.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>For you are a people holy to the Lord your God. He has chosen you to be his people, prized above all others on the face of the earth.

elements.question: The people of God are called to live distinctively, as Deuteronomy 7:6 says of Israel. Where are we most vulnerable to compromise, theologically or practically? What from the world around us is quietly enticing us away from wholehearted love for Jesus?
elements.questionHint: Ask where in your life gradual accommodation is happening that you have not yet named.

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>It is not because you were more numerous than all the other peoples that the Lord favored and chose you – for in fact you were the least numerous of all peoples. <sup>8</sup>Rather it is because of his love for you and his faithfulness to the promise he solemnly vowed to your ancestors that the Lord brought you out with great power, redeeming you from the place of slavery, from the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

elements.question: What does it mean for you personally that God chose his people, as Deuteronomy 7:7–8 says, not because of anything in them but purely because of his love? How does that truth speak to any sense of unworthiness or self-sufficiency you carry?
elements.questionHint: Ask whether being chosen despite being small makes God’s love more or less impressive to you.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 8: Remember the Lord’s Provision and Beware of Prosperity

elements.text: Chapter 7 told the people not to compromise with the world around them. Chapter 8 addresses a different and more subtle danger — the one that comes not from outside pressure but from within: the danger of forgetting God precisely when things are going well.

As you read, watch for the remarkable reframing Moses offers of the wilderness years — and the very specific spiritual warning he sounds about what prosperity does to a person’s relationship with God.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
1You must keep carefully all these commandments I am giving you today so that you may live, increase in number, and go in and occupy the land that the Lord promised to your ancestors. 2Remember the whole way by which he has brought you these forty years through the wilderness so that he might, by humbling you, test you to see if you have it within you to keep his commandments or not. 3So he humbled you by making you hungry and then feeding you with unfamiliar manna. He did this to teach you that humankind cannot live by bread alone, but also by everything that comes from the Lord’s mouth. 4Your clothing did not wear out nor did your feet swell all these forty years. 5Be keenly aware that just as a parent disciplines his child, so the Lord your God disciplines you. 6So you must keep his commandments, live according to his standards, and revere him. 7For the Lord your God is bringing you to a good land, a land of brooks, springs, and fountains flowing forth in valleys and hills, 8a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates, of olive trees and honey, 9a land where you may eat food in plenty and find no lack of anything, a land whose stones are iron and from whose hills you can mine copper. 10You will eat your fill and then praise the Lord your God because of the good land he has given you.

11Be sure you do not forget the Lord your God by not keeping his commandments, ordinances, and statutes that I am giving you today. 12When you eat your fill, when you build and occupy good houses, 13when your cattle and flocks increase, when you have plenty of silver and gold, and when you have abundance of everything, 14be sure you do not feel self-important and forget the Lord your God who brought you from the land of Egypt, the place of slavery, 15and who brought you through the great, fearful wilderness of venomous serpents and scorpions, an arid place with no water. He made water flow from a flint rock and 16fed you in the wilderness with manna (which your ancestors had never before known) so that he might by humbling you test you and eventually bring good to you. 17Be careful not to say, “My own ability and skill have gotten me this wealth.” 18You must remember the Lord your God, for he is the one who gives ability to get wealth; if you do this he will confirm his covenant that he made by oath to your ancestors, even as he has to this day. 19Now if you forget the Lord your God at all and follow other gods, worshiping and prostrating yourselves before them, I testify to you today that you will surely be annihilated. 20Just like the nations the Lord is about to destroy from your sight, so he will do to you because you would not obey him.

elements.question: Before working through the passage, what stands out to you in how Moses describes both the wilderness years and the abundant land they are about to enter? What is the emotional temperature of the chapter?

elements.text: 8:1-5: The Lord Disciplines His Children

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>You must keep carefully all these commandments I am giving you today so that you may live, increase in number, and go in and occupy the land that the Lord promised to your ancestors. <sup>2</sup>Remember the whole way by which he has brought you these forty years through the desert so that he might, by humbling you, test you to see if you have it within you to keep his commandments or not. <sup>3</sup>So he humbled you by making you hungry and then feeding you with unfamiliar manna. He did this to teach you that humankind cannot live by bread alone, but also by everything that comes from the Lord’s mouth. <sup>4</sup>Your clothing did not wear out nor did your feet swell all these forty years. <sup>5</sup>Be keenly aware that just as a parent disciplines his child, the Lord your God disciplines you.

elements.question: How does Moses reframe the forty years in the wilderness (vv2–5), and what was God doing when he let them go hungry and then fed them?
elements.sampleAnswer: In chapters 1–3 the wilderness looked mainly like punishment; here Moses presents it as education. God humbled the people by letting them hunger and then fed them with manna, to teach them that human beings do not live by bread alone but by everything that comes from the Lord’s mouth. Hunger exposes dependence in a way a full stomach never does. The father-son picture in v5 shows this as correction with care, aimed at forming them, not destroying them.
elements.questionHint: Look at the order in v3 (hunger first, then manna) and at the father-and-son picture in v5.

deeper.label: Go deeper…
deeper.question: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3 in his wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:4) — ‘man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’ How does Jesus’ use of this verse shed light on what it meant in Deuteronomy? And what does it tell us about Jesus himself that he lives out in his temptation what Israel failed to live out in theirs?

elements.mainPoint: The wilderness was **a classroom, not just a punishment**: God taught his people to live on his word.

elements.text: 8:6-20: Remember the Lord’s Provision and Beware of Prosperity

elements.passageText: <sup>6</sup>So you must keep his commandments, live according to his standards, and revere him. <sup>7</sup>For the Lord your God is bringing you to a good land, a land of brooks, springs, and fountains flowing forth in valleys and hills, <sup>8</sup>a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates, of olive trees and honey, <sup>9</sup>a land where you may eat food in plenty and find no lack of anything, a land whose stones are iron and from whose hills you can mine copper. <sup>10</sup>You will eat your fill and then praise the Lord your God because of the good land he has given you. <sup>11</sup>Be sure you do not forget the Lord your God by not keeping his commandments, ordinances, and statutes that I am giving you today. <sup>12</sup>When you eat your fill, when you build and occupy good houses, <sup>13</sup>when your cattle and flocks increase, when you have plenty of silver and gold, and when you have abundance of everything, <sup>14</sup>be sure you do not feel self-important and forget the Lord your God who brought you from the land of Egypt, the place of slavery, <sup>15</sup>and who brought you through the great, fearful desert of venomous serpents and scorpions, an arid place with no water. He made water flow from a flint rock and <sup>16</sup>fed you in the desert with manna (which your ancestors had never before known) so that he might by humbling you test you and eventually bring good to you. <sup>17</sup>Be careful not to say, ‘My own ability and skill have gotten me this wealth.’ <sup>18</sup>You must remember the Lord your God, for he is the one who gives ability to get wealth; if you do this he will confirm his covenant that he made by oath to your ancestors, even as he has to this day.

elements.question: What is the step by which prosperity leads to forgetting God, according to vv11–17?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses traces a realistic sequence: they will eat their fill, build good houses, see their herds and silver and gold increase, and then their hearts will become proud and they will forget the Lord. The critical step is the thought in v17 that their own strength and power have produced all this. It is not dramatic rejection of God but a quiet shift to self-attribution, in which God becomes irrelevant or a background figure in a story about them. Moses’ counter in v18 is that it is the Lord who gives the ability to produce wealth, so even our skills and opportunities are gifts.
elements.questionHint: Look for the thought in v17 that Moses is targeting.
elements.mainPoint: Prosperity leads to forgetting when we **credit our own strength** for what is really the Lord’s gift.

elements.question: According to this chapter, what is at the heart of Israel’s sin, and how can pride and self-sufficiency work as a form of idolatry?
elements.sampleAnswer: The sin at the heart of the chapter is forgetfulness of a particular kind: forgetting that we are not the source of what we have. Moses is not against enjoying God’s gifts, since v10 tells them to bless the Lord for the good land. He is against treating gifts as achievements and moving the centre of the story from God to self. That is a form of idolatry, because it raises self to the place that belongs to God. It shows when security rests in our finances, worth in our productivity, or decisions in our own judgment rather than in God.
elements.questionHint: Ask what it would look like to remember the Lord in the middle of abundance.
keyTerms: idol|take the place of god|in place of god|lord of
elements.mainPoint: Self-sufficiency is idolatry because it **puts the self where God belongs** as the source of what we have.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>2</sup>Remember the whole way by which he has brought you these forty years through the desert so that he might, by humbling you, test you to see if you have it within you to keep his commandments or not. <sup>3</sup>So he humbled you by making you hungry and then feeding you with unfamiliar manna. He did this to teach you that humankind cannot live by bread alone, but also by everything that comes from the Lord’s mouth.

elements.question: Moses commands deliberate remembering of the whole way God has led — including the difficult parts. Looking back at your own journey with God, what has the ‘manna in the desert’ been for you? What has God provided in a period of difficulty or lack that you are in danger of forgetting?
elements.questionHint: Ask what a period of difficulty or limitation has shown you about your dependence on God that comfort and success might have hidden.

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup>Be careful not to say, ‘My own ability and skill have gotten me this wealth.’ <sup>18</sup>You must remember the Lord your God, for he is the one who gives ability to get wealth; if you do this he will confirm his covenant that he made by oath to your ancestors, even as he has to this day.

elements.question: When are you most likely to become proud and self-satisfied, and to slide into the thought of Deuteronomy 8:17 without realising it? What practices of remembering and dependence help you resist that drift?
elements.questionHint: Ask where in your own story the narrative of ‘I did this’ is most active.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 9:1-10:11: You Will Not Enter the Land Because You Are Better — Rely on Your Mediator

elements.text: Chapter 9 completes the triad of chapters 7-9 — the three expansions of the Shema’s call to wholehearted love. Not compromising with the world around you (ch 7). Not forgetting God in prosperity (ch 8). And now, the most searching of all: not imagining that you deserve what God gives you.

As you read, watch for the specific wrong thinking Moses is heading off — and for the remarkable figure of Moses himself, who stands between an angry God and a guilty people, and pleads from God’s own character rather than the people’s.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
1Listen, Israel: Today you are about to cross the Jordan so you can dispossess the nations there, people greater and stronger than you who live in large cities with extremely high fortifications. 2They include the Anakites, a numerous and tall people whom you know about and of whom it is said, “Who is able to resist the Anakites?” 3Understand today that the Lord your God who goes before you is a devouring fire; he will defeat and subdue them before you. You will dispossess and destroy them quickly just as he has told you. 4Do not think to yourself after the Lord your God has driven them out before you, “Because of my own righteousness the Lord has brought me here to possess this land.” It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord is driving them out ahead of you. 5It is not because of your righteousness, or even your inner uprightness, that you have come here to possess their land. Instead, because of the wickedness of these nations, the Lord your God is driving them out ahead of you in order to confirm the promise he made on oath to your ancestors, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. 6Understand, therefore, that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God is about to give you this good land as a possession, for you are a stubborn people!

7Remember—don’t ever forget —how you provoked the Lord your God in the wilderness; from the time you left the land of Egypt until you came to this place you were constantly rebelling against him. 8At Horeb you provoked him and he was angry enough with you to destroy you. 9When I went up the mountain to receive the stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant that the Lord made with you, I remained there forty days and nights, eating and drinking nothing. 10The Lord gave me the two stone tablets, written by the very finger of God, and on them was everything he said to you at the mountain from the midst of the fire at the time of that assembly. 11Now at the end of the forty days and nights the Lord presented me with the two stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant. 12And he said to me, “Get up, go down at once from here because your people whom you brought out of Egypt have sinned! They have quickly turned from the way I commanded them and have made for themselves a cast metal image.” 13Moreover, he said to me, “I have taken note of these people; they are a stubborn lot! 14Stand aside and I will destroy them, obliterating their very name from memory, and I will make you into a stronger and more numerous nation than they are.”

15So I turned and went down the mountain while it was blazing with fire; the two tablets of the covenant were in my hands. 16When I looked, you had indeed sinned against the Lord your God and had cast for yourselves a metal calf; you had quickly turned aside from the way he had commanded you! 17I grabbed the two tablets, threw them down, and shattered them before your very eyes. 18Then I again fell down before the Lord for forty days and nights; I ate and drank nothing because of all the sin you had committed, doing such evil before the Lord as to enrage him. 19For I was terrified at the Lord’s intense anger that threatened to destroy you. But he listened to me this time as well. 20The Lord was also angry enough at Aaron to kill him, but at that time I prayed for him too. 21As for your sinful thing that you had made, the calf, I took it, melted it down, ground it up until it was as fine as dust, and tossed the dust into the stream that flows down the mountain. 22Moreover, you continued to provoke the Lord at Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth Hattaavah. 23And when he sent you from Kadesh Barnea and told you, “Go up and possess the land I have given you,” you rebelled against the Lord your God and would neither believe nor obey him. 24You have been rebelling against him from the very first day I knew you!

25I lay flat on the ground before the Lord for forty days and nights, for he had said he would destroy you. 26I prayed to him: O, Sovereign Lord, do not destroy your people, your valued property that you have powerfully redeemed, whom you brought out of Egypt by your strength. 27Remember your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; ignore the stubbornness, wickedness, and sin of these people. 28Otherwise the people of the land from which you brought us will say, “The Lord was unable to bring them to the land he promised them, and because of his hatred for them he has brought them out to kill them in the wilderness.” 29They are your people, your valued property, whom you brought out with great strength and power.

10:1At that same time the Lord said to me, “Carve out for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones and come up the mountain to me; also make for yourself a wooden ark. 2I will write on the tablets the same words that were on the first tablets you broke, and you must put them into the ark.” 3So I made an ark of acacia wood and carved out two stone tablets just like the first ones. Then I went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hands. 4The Lord then wrote on the tablets the same words, the Ten Commandments, which he had spoken to you at the mountain from the middle of the fire at the time of that assembly, and he gave them to me. 5Then I turned, went down the mountain, and placed the tablets into the ark I had made—they are still there, just as the Lord commanded me.

6During those days the Israelites traveled from Beeroth Bene Jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died and was buried, and his son Eleazar became priest in his place. 7From there they traveled to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a place of flowing streams. 8At that time the Lord set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the Lord’s covenant, to stand before the Lord to serve him, and to formulate blessings in his name, as they do to this very day. 9Therefore Levi has no allotment or inheritance among his brothers; the Lord is his inheritance just as the Lord your God told him. 10As for me, I stayed at the mountain as I did the first time, forty days and nights. The Lord listened to me that time as well and decided not to destroy you. 11Then he said to me, “Get up, set out leading the people so they may go and possess the land I promised to give to their ancestors.”

elements.question: Before looking at the details, what is the emotional tone of this passage? What do you notice about how Moses speaks to the people here compared with previous chapters?

elements.text: 9:1-6: Not Because of Your Righteousness

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>Listen, Israel: Today you are about to cross the Jordan so you can dispossess the nations there, people greater and stronger than you who live in large cities with extremely high fortifications. <sup>2</sup>They include the Anakites, a numerous and tall people whom you know about and of whom it is said, ‘Who is able to resist the Anakites?’ <sup>3</sup>Understand today that the Lord your God who goes before you is a devouring fire; he will defeat and subdue them before you. You will dispossess and destroy them quickly just as he has told you. <sup>4</sup>Do not think to yourself after the Lord your God has driven them out before you, ‘Because of my own righteousness the Lord has brought me here to possess this land.’ It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord is driving them out ahead of you. <sup>5</sup>It is not because of your righteousness, or even your inner uprightness, that you have come here to possess their land. Instead, because of the wickedness of these nations the Lord your God is driving them out ahead of you in order to confirm the promise he made on oath to your ancestors, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. <sup>6</sup>Understand, therefore, that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God is about to give you this good land as a possession, for you are a stubborn people!

elements.question: What wrong thinking does Moses rule out in vv4–6, and what does he give as the real grounds for the gift of the land?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses rules out the thought that the Lord is bringing Israel into the land because of their own righteousness, and he says so three times. The land is given because of the wickedness of the nations being driven out and because of the Lord’s oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Both grounds lie outside Israel. Moses closes the door on pride before it can open, since a people who think they are blessed because they are righteous will become proud and careless, while a people who know they are a stubborn people will cling to the God whose grace is their only standing.
elements.questionHint: Notice how often Moses says it is not because of Israel’s righteousness.
keyTerms: not because|not on account|not your righteousness|righteous
elements.mainPoint: Israel receives the land **not because of its righteousness** but because of the nations’ wickedness and God’s promise.

elements.text: 9:7-21: Remember Your Rebellion

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>Remember – don’t ever forget – how you provoked the Lord your God in the desert; from the time you left the land of Egypt until you came to this place you were constantly rebelling against him. <sup>8</sup>At Horeb you provoked him and he was angry enough with you to destroy you. <sup>9</sup>When I went up the mountain to receive the stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant that the Lord made with you, I remained there forty days and nights, eating and drinking nothing. <sup>10</sup>The Lord gave me the two stone tablets, written by the very finger of God, and on them was everything he said to you at the mountain from the midst of the fire at the time of that assembly. <sup>11</sup>Now at the end of the forty days and nights the Lord presented me with the two stone tablets, the tablets of the covenant. <sup>12</sup>And he said to me, ‘Get up, go down at once from here because your people whom you brought out of Egypt have sinned! They have quickly turned from the way I commanded them and have made for themselves a cast metal image.’ <sup>13</sup>Moreover, he said to me, ‘I have taken note of these people; they are a stubborn lot!’ <sup>14</sup>Stand aside and I will destroy them, obliterating their very name from memory, and I will make you into a stronger and more numerous nation than they are. <sup>15</sup>So I turned and went down the mountain while it was blazing with fire; the two tablets of the covenant were in my hands. <sup>16</sup>When I looked, you had indeed sinned against the Lord your God and had cast for yourselves a metal calf; you had quickly turned aside from the way he had commanded you! <sup>17</sup>I grabbed the two tablets, threw them down, and shattered them before your very eyes. <sup>18</sup>Then I again fell down before the Lord for forty days and nights; I ate and drank nothing because of all the sin you had committed, doing such evil before the Lord as to enrage him. <sup>19</sup>For I was terrified at the Lord’s intense anger that threatened to destroy you. But he listened to me this time as well. <sup>20</sup>The Lord was also angry enough at Aaron to kill him, but at that time I prayed for him too. <sup>21</sup>As for your sinful thing that you had made, the calf, I took it, melted it down, ground it up until it was as fine as dust, and tossed the dust into the stream that flows down the mountain.

elements.question: What makes the timing of the golden calf so shocking (vv7–21), and what does it show about Israel’s problem?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses was on the mountain for forty days receiving the tablets of the covenant while the people at its foot made a golden calf. The failure did not come after a long spell of complacency; it happened at the moment the covenant was being established. The people turned aside quickly from the way the Lord had commanded. This is a failure of the heart, not of knowledge or opportunity: they could not stay loyal to a God they had just seen descend in fire. They are a stubborn people.
elements.questionHint: Notice where Moses was and what he was receiving when the people turned aside (vv9–12).

deeper.label: Go deeper...
deeper.question: Moses fasted for forty days twice — once receiving the law, once interceding after the golden calf. The New Testament records that Jesus also fasted for forty days in the wilderness before facing temptation. What might the parallel suggest about Jesus in relation to Israel’s failure? How does Jesus’ response in Matthew 4 contrast with Israel’s pattern throughout the wilderness?

elements.mainPoint: The golden calf came **while the covenant was being given**, showing that Israel’s problem was a stubborn heart.

elements.text: 9:25-10:11: Rebellious People Need a Mediator

elements.passageText: <sup>9:25</sup>I lay flat on the ground before the Lord for forty days and nights, for he had said he would destroy you. <sup>26</sup>I prayed to him: O, Lord God, do not destroy your people, your valued property that you have powerfully redeemed, whom you brought out of Egypt by your strength. <sup>27</sup>Remember your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; ignore the stubbornness, wickedness, and sin of these people. <sup>28</sup>Otherwise the people of the land from which you brought us will say, ‘The Lord was unable to bring them to the land he promised them, and because of his hatred for them he has brought them out to kill them in the desert.’ <sup>29</sup>They are your people, your valued property, whom you brought out with great strength and power. <sup>10:1</sup>At that same time the Lord said to me, ‘Carve out for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones and come up the mountain to me; also make for yourself a wooden ark. <sup>2</sup>I will write on the tablets the same words that were on the first tablets you broke, and you must put them into the ark.’ <sup>3</sup>So I made an ark of acacia wood and carved out two stone tablets just like the first ones. Then I went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hands. <sup>4</sup>The Lord then wrote on the tablets the same words, the ten commandments, which he had spoken to you at the mountain from the middle of the fire at the time of that assembly, and he gave them to me. <sup>5</sup>Then I turned, went down the mountain, and placed the tablets into the ark I had made – they are still there, just as the Lord commanded me.

elements.question: What is the basis of Moses’ appeal to God in 9:26–29, and what does he not argue?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses does not argue that the people are good, that they deserve another chance or that their sin was understandable; he has just spent verses showing how stubborn they are. He argues from God’s own character and commitments: they are your people and your inheritance, whom you redeemed; remember Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; and think what the nations will say about you. The whole appeal rests on God’s purposes and reputation, not on human merit.
elements.questionHint: Look at what Moses calls the people in v26, whom he asks God to remember in v27, and what the nations might say in v28.

deeper.label: Go deeper...
deeper.question: Read Hebrews 7:25 and Romans 8:34. How does the New Testament describe Christ’s ongoing intercession for believers? What do you see that is similar to Moses’ intercession here — and what is different about what Christ does?

elements.mainPoint: Moses prays **on the ground of who God is**, not who Israel is.

elements.question: What does God do in response to Moses’ prayer in 10:1–5, and what is significant about the covenant he gives?
elements.sampleAnswer: God reissues the covenant in full. He tells Moses to cut new tablets like the first and writes on them the same words, and Moses puts them in the ark. Nothing is reduced or made probationary after Israel’s catastrophic failure. The response to their worst sin is complete restoration, and the ark holding the same tablets is a physical sign that the covenant stands undiminished.
elements.questionHint: Compare what God tells Moses to cut and write in 10:1–2 with what was on the first tablets.
elements.mainPoint: After the golden calf God **restores the covenant in full**, with the same words on new tablets.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>When the Lord your God drives them out before you, do not think to yourself, ‘Because of my own righteousness the Lord has brought me in to possess this land.’ It is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord is driving them out before you. <sup>5</sup>It is not because of your righteousness or your good conscience that you are going in to possess their land. Instead, it is because of their wickedness that the Lord your God is driving them out before you, in order to fulfill the promise he swore to your ancestors, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. <sup>6</sup>Understand, then, that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stubborn people!

elements.question: When do we compare ourselves with people we think of as more sinful and use that comparison to feel secure before God (Deuteronomy 9:4–6)? What does the New Testament say about our righteousness, and what does it offer instead?
elements.questionHint: Ask where you are tempted to read God’s blessing as evidence of your righteousness rather than his grace.

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup>I prayed to the Lord and said, ‘Lord God, do not destroy your people, your valued property that you have redeemed through your greatness and that you have brought out of Egypt by your strength. <sup>27</sup>Remember your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; ignore the stubbornness, wickedness, and sin of this people.’

elements.question: Moses intercedes (Deuteronomy 9:26–27) for a people he knows are guilty, on the basis of who God is rather than who they are. How does this shape the way we pray for ourselves and for others, especially when the sin is obvious and the guilt is real?
elements.questionHint: Ask whether guilt disqualifies you from coming to God, given that Moses prays honestly for a people whose sin he has just described.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 10:12-11:32: What Does the Lord Ask of You?

elements.text: Moses has established the theological foundations: the Commandments, the Shema, and the three threats to wholehearted love. Now, in this transitional passage before the detailed legal code begins, he draws the threads together into a single sweeping question: what does the Lord actually ask of you?
As you read, notice both the comprehensiveness of God’s demand and the character of the God who makes it — including his surprising attention to those whom the world overlooks.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
12Now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you except to revere him, to obey all his commandments, to love him, to serve him with all your mind and being, 13and to keep the Lord’s commandments and statutes that I am giving you today for your own good? 14The heavens—indeed the highest heavens—belong to the Lord your God, as does the earth and everything in it. 15However, only to your ancestors did he show his loving favor, and he chose you, their descendants, from all peoples—as is apparent today. 16Therefore, cleanse your hearts and stop being so stubborn! 17For the Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God who is unbiased and takes no bribe, 18who justly treats the orphan and widow, and who loves resident foreigners, giving them food and clothing. 19So you must love the resident foreigner because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. 20Revere the Lord your God, serve him, be loyal to him, and take oaths only in his name. 21He is the one you should praise; he is your God, the one who has done these great and awesome things for you that you have seen. 22When your ancestors went down to Egypt, they numbered only seventy, but now the Lord your God has made you as numerous as the stars of the sky.

11:1You must love the Lord your God and do what he requires; keep his statutes, ordinances, and commandments at all times. 2Bear in mind today that I am not speaking to your children who have not personally experienced the judgments of the Lord your God, which revealed his greatness, strength, and power. 3They did not see the awesome deeds he performed in the midst of Egypt against Pharaoh king of Egypt and his whole land, 4or what he did to the army of Egypt, including their horses and chariots, when he made the waters of the Red Sea overwhelm them while they were pursuing you and he annihilated them. 5They did not see what he did to you in the wilderness before you reached this place, 6or what he did to Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab the Reubenite, when the earth opened its mouth in the middle of the Israelite camp and swallowed them, their families, their tents, and all the property they brought with them. 7I am speaking to you because you are the ones who saw with your own eyes all the great deeds of the Lord.

8Now pay attention to all the commandments I am giving you today, so that you may be strong enough to enter and possess the land where you are headed, 9and that you may enjoy long life in the land the Lord promised to give to your ancestors and their descendants, a land flowing with milk and honey. 10For the land where you are headed is not like the land of Egypt from which you came, a land where you planted seed and which you irrigated by hand like a vegetable garden. 11Instead, the land you are crossing the Jordan to occupy is one of hills and valleys, a land that drinks in water from the rains, 12a land the Lord your God looks after. He is constantly attentive to it from the beginning to the end of the year. 13Now, if you pay close attention to my commandments that I am giving you today and love the Lord your God and serve him with all your mind and being, 14then he promises, “I will send rain for your land in its season, the autumn and the spring rains, so that you may gather in your grain, new wine, and olive oil. 15I will provide pasture for your livestock and you will eat your fill.”

16Make sure you do not turn away to serve and worship other gods! 17Then the anger of the Lord will erupt against you, and he will close up the sky so that it does not rain. The land will not yield its produce, and you will soon be removed from the good land that the Lord is about to give you. 18Fix these words of mine into your mind and being, tie them as a reminder on your hands, and let them be symbols on your forehead. 19Teach them to your children and speak of them as you sit in your house, as you walk along the road, as you lie down, and as you get up. 20Inscribe them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates 21so that your days and those of your descendants may be extended in the land that the Lord promised to give to your ancestors, like the days of heaven itself. 22For if you carefully observe all of these commandments I am giving you and love the Lord your God, live according to his standards, and remain loyal to him, 23then he will drive out all these nations ahead of you, and you will dispossess nations greater and stronger than you. 24Every place you set your foot will be yours; your border will extend from the desert to Lebanon and from the River (that is, the Euphrates) as far as the Mediterranean Sea. 25Nobody will be able to resist you; the Lord your God will spread the fear and terror of you over the whole land on which you walk, just as he promised you.

26Take note—I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse: 27the blessing if you take to heart the commandments of the Lord your God that I am giving you today, 28and the curse if you pay no attention to his commandments and turn from the way I am setting before you today to pursue other gods you have not known. 29When the Lord your God brings you into the land you are to possess, you must pronounce the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. 30Are they not across the Jordan River, toward the west, in the land of the Canaanites who live in the rift valley opposite Gilgal near the oak of Moreh? 31For you are about to cross the Jordan to possess the land the Lord your God is giving you, and you will possess and inhabit it. 32Be certain to keep all the statutes and ordinances that I am presenting to you today.

elements.question: Moses opens with a direct question: ‘What does the Lord your God require of you?’ Before looking at his answer, what would you have said if someone asked you that question?

elements.text: 10:12-22: Fear the Lord and Hold Fast to Him

elements.passageText: <sup>12</sup>Now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you except to revere him, to obey all his commandments, to love him, to serve him with all your mind and being, <sup>13</sup>and to keep the Lord’s commandments and statutes that I am giving you today for your own good? <sup>14</sup>The heavens – indeed the highest heavens – belong to the Lord your God, as does the earth and everything in it. <sup>15</sup>However, only to your ancestors did he show his loving favor, and he chose you, their descendants, from all peoples – as is apparent today. <sup>16</sup>Therefore, cleanse your heart and stop being so stubborn! <sup>17</sup>For the Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God who is unbiased and takes no bribe, <sup>18</sup>who justly treats the orphan and widow, and who loves resident foreigners, giving them food and clothing. <sup>19</sup>So you must love the resident foreigner because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. <sup>20</sup>Revere the Lord your God, serve him, be loyal to him and take oaths only in his name. <sup>21</sup>He is the one you should praise; he is your God, the one who has done these great and awesome things for you that you have seen. <sup>22</sup>When your ancestors went down to Egypt, they numbered only seventy, but now the Lord your God has made you as numerous as the stars of the sky.

elements.question: Moses gives a fivefold answer in vv12–13. What does each requirement add, and what single life do they describe together?
elements.sampleAnswer: The five requirements are facets of one whole-of-life orientation to the Lord, not five separate departments. To revere him is to give no one greater authority in your life, and to follow his ways is to respond to him in everything. To love him is the Shema again, and to serve him is wholehearted engagement rather than passive acknowledgement. To keep his commands is the practical expression of love and reverence. They reinforce one another, so Moses describes not a checklist but a person whose whole life is set towards the Lord.
elements.questionHint: Try reading the five requirements as one continuous description rather than five separate tasks.
elements.mainPoint: What the Lord asks is **one whole-hearted life** of reverence, obedience, love and service, not a checklist.

elements.question: What does Moses’ pairing of the greatness of God (v14) with his care for the orphan, widow and foreigner (vv17–18) reveal about God’s character?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses first establishes the scale of God’s sovereignty: the heavens, even the highest heaven, and the earth with all it contains belong to the Lord. Then he says that this same God treats the orphan and widow justly and loves the foreigner, giving them food and clothing. The greatest God is the one who attends to those everyone else overlooks, and the two are not in tension. This counters any power that exploits the vulnerable and grounds the command in v19: love the foreigner because God does, and because you were foreigners in Egypt.
elements.questionHint: Notice what v17 says about God’s greatness and what it says immediately after.
elements.mainPoint: The God who owns everything **pays special attention to those who have nothing**.

elements.text: 11:1-21: Love the Lord and Fix His Word in Your Heart

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>You must love the Lord your God and do what he requires; keep his statutes, ordinances, and commandments at all times. <sup>2</sup>Bear in mind today that I am not speaking to your children who have not personally experienced the judgments of the Lord your God, which revealed his greatness, strength, and power. <sup>3</sup>They did not see the awesome deeds he performed in the midst of Egypt against Pharaoh king of Egypt and his whole land, <sup>4</sup>or what he did to the army of Egypt, including their horses and chariots, when he made the waters of the Red Sea overwhelm them while they were pursuing you and he annihilated them. <sup>5</sup>They did not see what he did to you in the desert before you reached this place, <sup>6</sup>or what he did to Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab the Reubenite, when the earth opened its mouth in the middle of the Israelite camp and swallowed them, their families, their tents, and all the property they brought with them. <sup>7</sup>I am speaking to you because you are the ones who saw all the great deeds of the Lord! <sup>8</sup>Now pay attention to all the commandments I am giving you today, so that you may be strong enough to enter and possess the land where you are headed, <sup>9</sup>and that you may enjoy long life in the land the Lord promised to give to your ancestors and their descendants, a land flowing with milk and honey. <sup>10</sup>For the land where you are headed is not like the land of Egypt from which you came, a land where you planted seed and which you irrigated by hand like a vegetable garden. <sup>11</sup>Instead, the land you are crossing the Jordan to occupy is one of hills and valleys, a land that drinks in water from the rains, <sup>12</sup>a land the Lord your God looks after. He is constantly attentive to it from the beginning to the end of the year.

elements.question: What does the contrast between Egypt and Canaan in 11:10–12 teach about trusting the Lord?
elements.sampleAnswer: Egypt was a land of human technique, watered by hand like a vegetable garden. Canaan drinks the rain from heaven, and the Lord looks after it from the beginning of the year to the end. To enter Canaan is to enter a land that depends on God rather than on skill, because Israel cannot irrigate its way out of drought. Moses has also reminded those who saw God’s deeds with their own eyes (vv2–7) that their love and obedience should rest on what they have personally witnessed. The land itself is a school of trust.
elements.questionHint: Notice how each land gets its water, and who looks after the land in v12.
elements.mainPoint: Canaan is **a land that teaches dependence**: it lives on rain from heaven, not on human effort.

elements.text: 11:26-32: Make Your Choice

elements.passageText: <sup>26</sup>Take note that I am setting before you today a blessing and a curse -- <sup>27</sup>the blessing if you take to heart the commandments of the Lord your God that I am giving you today, <sup>28</sup>and the curse if you do not take to heart the commandments of the Lord your God, but turn from the way I am commanding you today and follow other gods you do not know.

elements.question: What choice does Moses set before the people in 11:26–28, and what does each outcome depend on?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses sets before the people a blessing and a curse. The blessing comes if they obey the commands of the Lord, and the curse if they do not obey but turn aside to other gods. The starkness is pastoral: there are only two paths, and he has made the character of the God behind the blessing as clear as he can. The choice should be obvious. The chapters that follow are there because, as the rest of the book shows, obedience is hard to practise in specific areas of life, even when the principle is clear.
elements.questionHint: Notice the two words Moses sets side by side and the condition attached to each.
elements.mainPoint: Moses puts before Israel **a clear choice between blessing and curse**, depending on obedience to the Lord.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>17</sup>For the Lord your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God who is unbiased and takes no bribe, <sup>18</sup>who justly treats the orphan and widow, and who loves resident foreigners, giving them food and clothing. <sup>19</sup>So you must love the resident foreigner because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

elements.question: God’s character is described as supremely great and yet attentive to the orphan, widow and foreigner (Deuteronomy 10:17–19). What does the Lord ask of us in light of this? Who are the overlooked and vulnerable in your context, and what would reflecting God’s attention to them look like in practice?
elements.questionHint: Ask how your own experience of vulnerability or being an outsider shapes the way you treat others in that position.

elements.passageText: <sup>16</sup>Therefore, cleanse your heart and stop being so stubborn!

elements.question: ‘Circumcise your hearts’ (Deuteronomy 10:16) is Moses’ image for the inward responsiveness to God that all the commands require. What does it mean to have a circumcised heart, and what is the New Testament promise about how that becomes possible?
elements.questionHint: Ask what the difference between a hard heart and a soft one looks like when God’s word asks something difficult of you.

deeper.label: Go deeper...
deeper.question: Read Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33, and Ezekiel 36:26-27. How do these passages develop the promise implied in 10:16? What do they say God will do about the heart problem that the law cannot fix from the outside?

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 12: Worship the Lord in His Place and in His Way

elements.text: With chapter 12, Moses’ second sermon shifts into its longest and most detailed section: the legal code of chapters 12-26. These are not bureaucratic regulations but the flesh on the bones of what loving God with everything actually looks like in daily life. Chapter 12 sets the foundation by addressing the most basic question of all: how is God to be worshipped?

As you read, pay attention to the positive vision of worship Moses describes — it is not austere or individualistic. And notice the foundational principle underneath the specific instructions that runs through the whole chapter.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
1These are the statutes and ordinances you must be careful to obey as long as you live in the land the Lord, the God of your ancestors, has given you to possess. 2You must by all means destroy all the places where the nations you are about to dispossess worship their gods—on the high mountains and hills and under every leafy tree. 3You must tear down their altars, shatter their sacred pillars, burn up their sacred Asherah poles, and cut down the images of their gods; you must eliminate their very memory from that place. 4You must not worship the Lord your God the way they worship. 5But you must seek only the place he chooses from all your tribes to establish his name as his place of residence, and you must go there. 6And there you must take your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the personal offerings you have prepared, your votive offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks. 7Both you and your families must feast there before the Lord your God and rejoice in all the output of your labor with which he has blessed you. 8You must not do as we are doing here today, with everyone doing what seems best to him, 9for you have not yet come to the final stop and inheritance the Lord your God is giving you. 10When you do go across the Jordan River and settle in the land he is granting you as an inheritance and you find relief from all the enemies who surround you, you will live in safety. 11Then you must come to the place the Lord your God chooses for his name to reside, bringing everything I am commanding you—your burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, the personal offerings you have prepared, and all your choice votive offerings that you devote to him. 12You shall rejoice in the presence of the Lord your God, along with your sons, daughters, male and female servants, and the Levites in your villages (since they have no allotment or inheritance with you). 13Make sure you do not offer burnt offerings in any place you wish, 14for you may do so only in the place the Lord chooses in one of your tribal areas—there you may do everything I am commanding you.

15On the other hand, you may slaughter and eat meat as you please when the Lord your God blesses you in all your villages. Both the ritually pure and impure may eat it, whether it is a gazelle or an ibex. 16However, you must not eat blood—pour it out on the ground like water. 17You will not be allowed to eat in your villages your tithe of grain, new wine, olive oil, the firstborn of your herd and flock, any votive offerings you have vowed, or your freewill and personal offerings. 18Only in the presence of the Lord your God may you eat these, in the place he chooses. This applies to you, your son, your daughter, your male and female servants, and the Levites in your villages. In that place you will rejoice before the Lord your God in all the output of your labor. 19Be careful not to overlook the Levites as long as you live in the land.

20When the Lord your God extends your borders as he said he would do and you say, “I want to eat meat just as I please,” you may do so as you wish. 21If the place he chooses to locate his name is too far for you, you may slaughter any of your herd and flock he has given you just as I have stipulated; you may eat them in your villages just as you wish. 22As you eat the gazelle or ibex, so you may eat these; the ritually impure and pure alike may eat them. 23However, by no means eat the blood, for the blood is life itself —you must not eat the life with the meat. 24You must not eat it! You must pour it out on the ground like water. 25You must not eat it so that it may go well with you and your children after you; you will be doing what is right in the Lord’s sight. 26But the holy things and votive offerings that belong to you, you must pick up and take to the place the Lord will choose. 27You must offer your burnt offerings, both meat and blood, on the altar of the Lord your God; the blood of your other sacrifices you must pour out on his altar while you eat the meat. 28Pay careful attention to all these things I am commanding you so that it may always go well with you and your children after you when you do what is good and right in the sight of the Lord your God.

29When the Lord your God eliminates the nations from the place where you are headed and you dispossess them, you will settle down in their land. 30After they have been destroyed from your presence, be careful not to be ensnared like they are; do not pursue their gods and say, “How do these nations serve their gods? I will do the same.” 31You must not worship the Lord your God the way they do! For everything that is abhorrent to him, everything he hates, they have done when worshiping their gods. They even burn up their sons and daughters before their gods!

elements.question: What is your initial reaction to a chapter about where and how to worship? Does it seem overly restrictive, or is there something else going on that you notice?

elements.text: 12:1-14: Worship the Lord in His Way

elements.passageText: <sup>1</sup>These are the statutes and ordinances you must be careful to obey as long as you live in the land the Lord, the God of your ancestors, has given you to possess. <sup>2</sup>You must by all means destroy all the places where the nations you are about to dispossess worship their gods – on the high mountains and hills and under every leafy tree. <sup>3</sup>You must tear down their altars, shatter their sacred pillars, burn up their sacred Asherah poles, and cut down the images of their gods; you must eliminate their very memory from that place. <sup>4</sup>You must not worship the Lord your God the way they worship. <sup>5</sup>But you must seek only the place he chooses from all your tribes to establish his name as his place of residence, and you must go there. <sup>6</sup>And there you must take your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the personal offerings you have prepared, your votive offerings, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks. <sup>7</sup>Both you and your families must feast there before the Lord your God and rejoice in all the output of your labor with which he has blessed you. <sup>8</sup>You must not do like we are doing here today, with everyone doing what seems best to him. <sup>9</sup>For you have not yet come to the final stop and inheritance the Lord your God is giving you. <sup>10</sup>When you do go across the Jordan River and settle in the land he is granting you as an inheritance and you find relief from all the enemies who surround you, you will live in safety. <sup>11</sup>Then you must come to the place the Lord your God chooses for his name to reside, bringing everything I am commanding you – your burnt offerings, sacrifices, tithes, the personal offerings you have prepared, and all your choice votive offerings which you devote to him. <sup>12</sup>You shall rejoice in the presence of the Lord your God, along with your sons, daughters, male and female servants, and the Levites in your villages (since they have no allotment or inheritance with you). <sup>13</sup>Make sure you do not offer burnt offerings in any place you wish. <sup>14</sup>For you may do so only in the place the Lord chooses in one of your tribal areas – there you may do everything I am commanding you.

elements.question: How are the Israelites not to worship, and what are they to do instead (vv1–14)? What does the repeated phrase about the place the Lord will choose establish?
elements.sampleAnswer: They are not to worship the Lord as the Canaanites worship their gods, at scattered high places and under green trees. Instead they are to worship at the one place the Lord will choose for his name. The repetition of this phrase stresses a single principle: God defines the terms of his own worship, so the worshipper does not choose where or how. This is not arbitrary restriction; it reflects that the Lord is not a projection of human religious instinct. Worship shaped by the worshipper’s preferences ends up worshipping something of the worshipper’s own making.
elements.questionHint: Notice how often Moses speaks of a place the Lord will choose, and what v8 says about doing what is right in one’s own eyes.
keyTerms: god defines|his terms|not our|own eyes|own opinion|how and where
elements.mainPoint: **God, not the worshipper, sets the terms of worship**: where, how and in what spirit.

elements.question: What positive picture of worship does Moses give in vv7 and 12?
elements.sampleAnswer: The picture is communal, joyful and abundant. The people eat before the Lord and rejoice in all that their labour has produced, with their households, because the Lord has blessed them (v7). Verse 12 widens the circle to include the Levite, who has no allotment of his own. This is not a grim, individual, duty-driven exercise but a feast shared with the whole household before a generous God. The restrictions in the chapter exist to protect this joyful feast from being corrupted by a very different kind of religion.
elements.questionHint: Look at what the people do before the Lord in v7 and who is included in the rejoicing in v12.
elements.mainPoint: Worship at the Lord’s place is **a joyful shared feast**, not a grim duty.

elements.text: 12:29-32: Do Not Worship Like the Nations

elements.passageText: <sup>29</sup>When the Lord your God eliminates the nations from the place where you are headed and you dispossess them, you will settle down in their land. <sup>30</sup>After they have been destroyed from your presence, be careful not to be ensnared like they are; do not pursue their gods and say, ‘How do these nations serve their gods? I will do the same.’ <sup>31</sup>You must not worship the Lord your God the way they do! For everything that is abhorrent to him, everything he hates, they have done when worshiping their gods. They even burn up their sons and daughters before their gods! <sup>32</sup>You must be careful to do everything I am commanding you. Do not add to it or subtract from it!

elements.question: Why does Moses warn against even enquiring how other nations worship their gods (vv29–31), and what does v31 show about where self-determined worship leads?
elements.sampleAnswer: Moses closes the door on curiosity as well as imitation. We cannot watch how others worship their gods without being shaped by it, so familiarity leads towards assimilation. Verse 31 gives the ultimate example: the nations even burn their sons and daughters in the fire to their gods. This shows that worship shaped by human preference rather than divine revelation has no limit. The chapter ends by returning to the foundation: do everything the Lord commands, adding nothing and subtracting nothing.
elements.questionHint: Look at the question Moses imagines the people asking in v30 and what the nations do in v31.
elements.mainPoint: Worship that follows human preference **has no limit**, which is why Moses forbids even curiosity about pagan worship.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: <sup>4</sup>You must not worship the Lord your God the way they worship. <sup>5</sup>Instead, you must seek only the place he chooses from all your tribes to establish his name as his place of residence, and you must go there.

elements.question: The principle of Deuteronomy 12 is that God defines the terms of his own worship, so that we come to him on his terms, not ours. How does the New Testament fulfil and transform this? Where is ‘the place the Lord has chosen’ for us to meet him today?
elements.questionHint: Ask what it means that Jesus, rather than a place, is now where we meet God.

deeper.label: Go deeper...
deeper.question: Read John 2:19-21, John 4:21-24, and John 14:6. How does John show Jesus fulfilling what the one place of worship in Deuteronomy 12 was pointing toward? What does this mean for how we understand both Christian worship and our access to God?

elements.passageText: <sup>7</sup>You must eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice in all the output of your labor, you and your households, in which the Lord your God has blessed you.

elements.question: The worship Moses describes in Deuteronomy 12:7 is communal and joyful, and in v12 it explicitly includes the Levite, the person without resources of their own. What would it look like for our gathered worship to reflect this same spirit?
elements.questionHint: Ask why Moses names the Levite explicitly, and what that person’s presence says about what the gathering is for.

chapters.chapterTitle: Deuteronomy 13:1-14:21: Loyalty to the Lord — Purge Evil and Be Holy

elements.text: Chapter 12 established how God is to be worshipped. Chapters 13-14 address the threats to that worship from within the community. Chapter 13 is among the most demanding passages in Deuteronomy — dealing with false teachers, intimate relationships, and the cancer-like spread of idolatry. Chapter 14 then turns to the daily, embodied distinctiveness that marks the people as belonging to the Lord.

As you read chapter 13, resist the urge to move past the discomfort too quickly. Moses intends you to feel the weight of what he is describing. The severity is not cruelty — it is a measure of how seriously idolatry must be taken.

elements.question: Read the passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
1Suppose a prophet or one who foretells by dreams should appear among you and show you a sign or wonder, 2and the sign or wonder should come to pass concerning what he said to you, namely, “Let us follow other gods”—gods whom you have not previously known—“and let us serve them.” 3You must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, for the Lord your God will be testing you to see if you love him with all your mind and being. 4You must follow the Lord your God and revere only him; and you must observe his commandments, obey him, serve him, and remain loyal to him. 5As for that prophet or dreamer, he must be executed because he encouraged rebellion against the Lord your God who brought you from the land of Egypt, redeeming you from that place of slavery, and because he has tried to entice you from the way the Lord your God has commanded you to go. In this way you must purge evil from among you.

6Suppose your own full brother, your son, your daughter, your beloved wife, or your closest friend should seduce you secretly and encourage you to go and serve other gods that neither you nor your ancestors have previously known, 7the gods of the surrounding people (whether near you or far from you, from one end of the earth to the other). 8You must not give in to him or even listen to him; do not feel sympathy for him or spare him or cover up for him. 9Instead, you must kill him without fail! Your own hand must be the first to strike him, and then the hands of the whole community. 10You must stone him to death because he tried to entice you away from the Lord your God, who delivered you from the land of Egypt, that place of slavery. 11Thus all Israel will hear and be afraid; no longer will they continue to do evil like this among you.

12Suppose you should hear in one of your cities, which the Lord your God is giving you as a place to live, that 13some evil people have departed from among you to entice the inhabitants of their cities, saying, “Let’s go and serve other gods” (whom you have not known before). 14You must investigate thoroughly and inquire carefully. If it is indeed true that such a disgraceful thing is being done among you, 15you must by all means slaughter the inhabitants of that city with the sword; annihilate with the sword everyone in it, as well as the livestock. 16You must gather all of its plunder into the middle of the plaza and burn the city and all its plunder as a whole burnt offering to the Lord your God. It will be an abandoned ruin forever—it must never be rebuilt again. 17You must not take for yourself anything that has been placed under judgment. Then the Lord will relent from his intense anger, show you compassion, have mercy on you, and multiply you as he promised your ancestors. 18Thus you must obey the Lord your God, keeping all his commandments that I am giving you today and doing what is right before him.

14:1You are children of the Lord your God. Do not cut yourselves or shave your forehead bald for the sake of the dead. 2For you are a people holy to the Lord your God. He has chosen you to be his people, prized above all others on the face of the earth.

3You must not eat any forbidden thing. 4These are the animals you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, 5the ibex, the gazelle, the deer, the wild goat, the antelope, the wild oryx, and the mountain sheep. 6You may eat any animal that has hooves divided into two parts and that chews the cud. 7However, you may not eat the following animals among those that chew the cud or those that have divided hooves: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger. (Although they chew the cud, they do not have divided hooves and are therefore ritually impure to you.) 8Also, the pig is ritually impure to you; though it has divided hooves, it does not chew the cud. You may not eat their meat or even touch their remains.
